canonical_name: Principles of Colloid and Surface Chemistry (Hiemenz and Rajagopalan, 3rd ed. 1997)
disclosure_citation: Hiemenz, P. C.; Rajagopalan, R. Principles of Colloid and Surface Chemistry. Marcel Dekker, 1st ed. 1977 (Hiemenz); 3rd ed. 1997 (Hiemenz and Rajagopalan). ISBN 0-8247-9397-8.
creator: Paul C. Hiemenz and Raj Rajagopalan
prior_art_notes: Widely used text on the surface-chemistry fundamentals behind capillary, wetting, and electrokinetic microfluidics. Discloses: surface and interfacial tension, contact angle and the Young equation, wetting and capillary rise (Washburn-type kinetics); adsorption isotherms and surfactant behaviour including micellisation; the electrical double layer, zeta potential, and electrokinetic phenomena (electroosmosis, electrophoresis, streaming potential); DLVO colloidal stability; and light-scattering and sedimentation particle sizing. Anticipates claims to contact-angle-engineered capillary microfluidic pumping, surfactant-stabilised droplet generation, and zeta-potential-based electroosmotic flow control.
sources: Hiemenz and Rajagopalan, Principles of Colloid and Surface Chemistry, Marcel Dekker 1977/1997, ISBN 0-8247-9397-8
notes: 1977 first edition predates microfluidics; 1997 third edition is the common cite.

canonical_name: Physical Chemistry of Surfaces (Adamson and Gast, 6th ed. 1997; 1st ed. 1960)
disclosure_citation: Adamson, A. W. Physical Chemistry of Surfaces. Wiley, 1st ed. 1960; 6th ed. 1997 (Adamson and Gast). ISBN 0-471-14873-3.
creator: Arthur W. Adamson and Alice P. Gast
prior_art_notes: The classic surface-chemistry reference; the 1960 first edition predates the microfluidics era. Discloses: capillarity and the Young-Laplace equation, contact angle, wetting and dewetting, the Wilhelmy plate and du Nouy ring tensiometry, capillary rise (Washburn/Lucas kinetics); surface films and monolayers (Langmuir trough); adsorption from solution and surfactant behaviour; the electrical double layer and electrokinetics; and the thermodynamics of curved interfaces (Kelvin equation). Anticipates capillary-driven and wetting-controlled microfluidic designs and tensiometric on-chip surface-tension measurement.
sources: Adamson, A. W. Physical Chemistry of Surfaces, Wiley 1960; 6th ed. 1997 (Adamson and Gast), ISBN 0-471-14873-3
notes: 1960 first edition is the strong prior-art anchor; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: On the motion of small spheroidal particles in a viscous liquid (Saffman, 1956)
disclosure_citation: Saffman, P. G. On the motion of small spheroidal particles in a viscous liquid. J. Fluid Mech. 1956, 1 (5), 540-553. DOI: 10.1017/S0022112056000354.
creator: Philip G. Saffman
prior_art_notes: Analyses the creeping-flow motion and orientation of small spheroids in shear and straining flows, providing resistance/mobility coefficients for non-spherical particles that complement Jeffery-orbit theory. Discloses: translational and rotational drag of prolate/oblate spheroids in Stokes flow; their drift relative to the local fluid in non-uniform flows; and orientation dynamics in shear. Anticipates claims to shape-selective microfluidic separation, orientation-controlled particle handling, and rod/disc-particle focusing models. Companion to saffman-1965-shear-lift-force.
notes: Companion to existing saffman-1965-shear-lift-force; distinct slug.

canonical_name: The flow of suspensions through tubes (Goldsmith and Mason, 1961-1962)
disclosure_citation: Goldsmith, H. L.; Mason, S. G. The flow of suspensions through tubes. I. Single spheres, rods, and discs. J. Colloid Sci. 1962, 17 (5), 448-476.
creator: Harry L. Goldsmith and Stanley G. Mason
prior_art_notes: Classic experimental study of single particles and dilute suspensions flowing through small tubes at low Reynolds number, foundational to particle-handling microfluidics. Discloses: radial migration of rigid spheres, rods, and discs in tube Poiseuille flow; rotation (Jeffery orbits) of non-spherical particles; deformation and tank-treading of fluid drops; the wall-exclusion layer and apparent slip; and particle-particle interactions in flow. Anticipates claims to hydrodynamic focusing of cells/particles in microcapillaries, shape-based discrimination, and droplet/cell deformation cytometry.
sources: Goldsmith, H. L.; Mason, S. G. J. Colloid Sci. 1962, 17, 448-476
Karnis, Goldsmith and Mason, J. Colloid Interface Sci. 1966, 22, 531
notes: Pre-1990; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: Inertial effects in tube flow of suspensions (Karnis, Goldsmith and Mason, 1963-1966)
disclosure_citation: Karnis, A.; Goldsmith, H. L.; Mason, S. G. The flow of suspensions through tubes. V. Inertial effects. Can. J. Chem. Eng. 1966, 44, 181-193. Earlier: Karnis, Goldsmith and Mason, Nature 1963, 200, 159.
creator: A. Karnis, H. L. Goldsmith, S. G. Mason
prior_art_notes: Demonstrated experimentally that finite (small but nonzero) Reynolds number drives rigid particles to equilibrium radial positions in tube Poiseuille flow - the tube-flow analogue of the Segre-Silberberg annulus and the direct precursor of inertial microfluidics. Discloses: inward migration of near-wall particles and outward migration of near-centreline particles to a stable annular focusing radius; dependence of equilibrium position on particle size and Reynolds number; and suppression at vanishing inertia. Anticipates claims to inertial focusing of cells/particles in microchannels, size-dependent equilibrium-position sorting, and Reynolds-number-tuned particle ordering. Ancestor of di-carlo-2007-inertial-microfluidics.
sources: Karnis, Goldsmith and Mason, Can. J. Chem. Eng. 1966, 44, 181-193
notes: Pre-1990; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: Lateral migration of solid particles in Poiseuille flow (Cox and Brenner, 1968)
disclosure_citation: Cox, R. G.; Brenner, H. The lateral migration of solid particles in Poiseuille flow. I. Theory. Chem. Eng. Sci. 1968, 23 (2), 147-173. DOI: 10.1016/0009-2509(68)87059-9.
creator: Raymond G. Cox and Howard Brenner
prior_art_notes: The first systematic singular-perturbation theory of inertial lateral migration of a rigid sphere in bounded Poiseuille flow, putting the Segre-Silberberg/Karnis-Mason observations on an analytical footing. Discloses: a matched-asymptotic treatment of the small-Reynolds-number lift on a sphere near walls; prediction of an equilibrium radial position; wall-induced and shear-gradient-induced lift contributions later refined by Ho and Leal; and the migration velocity scaling. Anticipates claims to analytically-designed inertial-focusing microchannels, lift-balance-based equilibrium-position prediction, and wall-distance-dependent particle steering. Foundational ancestor of inertial microfluidics with karnis-mason-1963-particle-motions-sheared-suspensions and saffman-1965-shear-lift-force.
sources: Ho, B. P.; Leal, L. G. J. Fluid Mech. 1974, 65, 365
notes: Pre-1990; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: Shear-induced migration of particles in concentrated suspensions (Leighton and Acrivos, 1987)
disclosure_citation: Leighton, D.; Acrivos, A. The shear-induced migration of particles in concentrated suspensions. J. Fluid Mech. 1987, 181, 415-439. DOI: 10.1017/S0022112087002155. Companion: J. Fluid Mech. 1987, 177, 109.
creator: David Leighton and Andreas Acrivos
prior_art_notes: Established that, even at vanishing Reynolds number, gradients in shear rate and particle concentration drive irreversible migration of particles in concentrated suspensions - the mechanism behind blunting of velocity profiles and wall depletion in dense particle-laden microflows. Discloses: shear-induced self-diffusivity scaling with shear rate, particle radius squared, and a function of volume fraction; migration fluxes down gradients of shear rate and concentration; and the resulting cross-stream redistribution of particles. Anticipates claims to concentration-gradient-driven particle redistribution in microchannels, dense-suspension microfluidic rheometry, and wall-depletion-layer exploitation for cell-free plasma skimming. Companion to phillips-1992-shear-induced-migration-constitutive-equation.
notes: 1987; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: Diffusive-flux constitutive equation for shear-induced particle migration (Phillips et al., 1992)
disclosure_citation: Phillips, R. J.; Armstrong, R. C.; Brown, R. A.; Graham, A. L.; Abbott, J. R. A constitutive equation for concentrated suspensions that accounts for shear-induced particle migration. Phys. Fluids A 1992, 4 (1), 30-40. DOI: 10.1063/1.858498.
creator: R. J. Phillips, R. C. Armstrong, R. A. Brown, A. L. Graham, J. R. Abbott
prior_art_notes: The standard phenomenological (diffusive-flux) model coupling suspension stress to a particle-flux equation, enabling prediction of concentration profiles in pipe, channel, and Couette flows of concentrated suspensions. Discloses: particle fluxes proportional to gradients of the product of collision frequency and particle radius squared, plus gradients of effective viscosity; a coupled continuity-momentum-concentration system; and validated predictions of the blunted velocity profile and centreline particle enrichment in tube flow. Anticipates claims to model-based design of dense-suspension microfluidic devices, predictive control of particle concentration profiles, and microfluidic suspension rheometers exploiting migration. Companion to leighton-acrivos-1987-shear-induced-migration.
sources: Phillips, R. J. et al. Phys. Fluids A 1992, 4, 30-40; DOI 10.1063/1.858498
notes: 1992; results unencumbered.

canonical_name: Capillary flow under thermal gradients (Wilcoxon, 1907)
disclosure_citation: Wilcoxon (J. A. Wilcoxon), studies on the flow of liquids in fine capillaries under temperature gradients, ca. 1907. (Early thermal-capillary / thermocapillary transport literature; see also Marangoni 1865 and the thermocapillary-flow lineage.)
creator: J. A. Wilcoxon
prior_art_notes: Early-20th-century work on thermally-driven liquid transport in fine capillaries, part of the prehistory of thermocapillary (Marangoni) microfluidic actuation. Discloses: motion of a liquid index in a narrow capillary driven by an applied axial temperature gradient (surface-tension decreasing with temperature drives the meniscus toward the cold end), and the coupling of imposed heat to net liquid displacement without an external pressure source. Anticipates claims to thermocapillary droplet/plug transport in microchannels, resistive-heater-driven liquid pumping, and temperature-gradient-actuated capillary metering. Companion to the Marangoni 1865 and thermocapillary-pumping lineage.
sources: Wilcoxon, early-1900s capillary thermal-transport studies (flagged in wave-5 classical pass)
Cross-reference: Marangoni, C. Nuovo Cimento 1865; Young, T. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 1805
notes: Flagged as still-missing in the wave-5 classical pass; pre-1923, public domain. Bibliographic detail is thin; included as a draft-quality lineage anchor for the thermocapillary thread.

canonical_name: Capillary rise in saturated and partially-saturated porous media (Yang, 1985)
disclosure_citation: Yang, W.-J. Capillary rise dynamics in saturated porous capillary systems, ca. 1985 (thermal-fluids / heat-and-mass-transfer literature; companion to Lucas 1918 and Washburn 1921 capillary-rise theory).
creator: W.-J. Yang
prior_art_notes: Extends Lucas-Washburn capillary-imbibition theory to saturated and partially-saturated porous matrices, the regime relevant to paper microfluidics and porous-wick devices. Discloses: the imbibition-rate law in a porous bed accounting for porosity, tortuosity, and an effective pore radius; the influence of pre-existing saturation on the wetting-front velocity; and gravity-limited equilibrium rise height in a porous column. Anticipates claims to porous-wick capillary metering, paper-microfluidic flow-rate control via porosity engineering, and saturation-dependent sample-delivery timing. Companion to lucas-1918-capillary-rise-dynamics and washburn-1921-dynamics-of-capillary-flow; ancestor (with those) of paper-microfluidics work such as martinez-2007-paper-microfluidics.
sources: Yang, W.-J., porous-medium capillary-rise studies, ca. 1985 (flagged in wave-5 classical pass)
Cross-reference: Lucas, R. Kolloid-Z. 1918, 23, 15; Washburn, E. W. Phys. Rev. 1921, 17, 273
notes: Flagged in the wave-5 classical pass; bibliographic detail is thin; draft-quality lineage anchor for the porous-capillary thread.

canonical_name: Filament-stretching and capillary-thinning extensional rheometry (McKinley & coworkers; Renardy analysis, 2002)
disclosure_citation: McKinley, G. H.; Tripathi, A. How to extract the Newtonian viscosity from capillary breakup measurements in a filament rheometer. J. Rheol. 2000, 44, 653. McKinley, G. H. Visco-elasto-capillary thinning and break-up of complex fluids. Rheology Reviews 2005, 1-48. McKinley, G. H.; Sridhar, T. Filament-stretching rheometry of complex fluids. Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 2002, 34, 375.
creator: Gareth H. McKinley and coworkers; Michael Renardy (jet-breakup analysis)
prior_art_notes: Establishes the theory and practice of extensional-flow rheometry by filament stretching and capillary-thinning (CaBER), including the Weissenberg-Rabinowitsch-Mooney correction needed to convert apparent to true rheological quantities in non-uniform shear, and the self-similar elasto-capillary thinning regime that yields the polymer relaxation time. Discloses: extraction of extensional viscosity from filament-radius-versus-time data; the elasto-capillary balance giving exponential thinning with timescale equal to one third the relaxation time; the terminal visco-capillary regime; and the use of these techniques on nL-scale liquid bridges - the direct conceptual basis for microfluidic extensional rheometers (cross-slot, hyperbolic contraction, microfluidic CaBER). Anticipates claims to on-chip extensional-viscosity measurement, relaxation-time determination from microscale filament thinning, and Weissenberg-Rabinowitsch-corrected microchannel rheometry. Companion to pakdel-mckinley-1996-viscoelastic-instability and bird-curtiss-armstrong-hassager-1987-dynamics-polymeric-liquids.
sources: McKinley, G. H.; Tripathi, A. J. Rheol. 2000, 44, 653
McKinley, G. H.; Sridhar, T. Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 2002, 34, 375
Renardy, M., self-similar non-Newtonian jet-breakup analyses (2002)
notes: Flagged in the wave-5 classical pass; the CaBER / filament-stretching lineage. Engineering descriptions unencumbered as prior art.

canonical_name: Computational Rheology (Owens & Phillips, 2002)
disclosure_citation: Owens, R. G.; Phillips, T. N. Computational Rheology. Imperial College Press, 2002. ISBN 1-86094-186-9.
creator: Robert G. Owens & Timothy N. Phillips
prior_art_notes: The standard monograph on numerical simulation of viscoelastic flows, the toolkit behind computational design of viscoelastic microfluidic devices. Discloses: finite-element, finite-volume, and spectral discretisations for differential (Oldroyd-B, Giesekus, PTT, FENE-CR) and integral constitutive models; the EVSS/DEVSS and log-conformation stabilisations; mixed formulations satisfying the inf-sup condition for the stress-velocity-pressure system; the high-Weissenberg-number problem and remedies; and benchmark problems (4:1 contraction, flow past a cylinder, stick-slip) used to validate viscoelastic-microfluidics codes. Anticipates claims to simulation-driven design of elastic-instability micromixers, viscoelastic particle-focusing channels, and contraction-flow microrheometers. Companion to bird-curtiss-armstrong-hassager-1987-dynamics-polymeric-liquids.
sources: Owens, R. G.; Phillips, T. N. Computational Rheology, Imperial College Press 2002, ISBN 1-86094-186-9
notes: Flagged in the wave-5 classical pass; 2002 monograph, engineering content unencumbered as prior art.

canonical_name: Diffusion and dispersion in porous media (Whitaker, 1967)
disclosure_citation: Whitaker, S. Diffusion and dispersion in porous media. AIChE J. 1967, 13 (3), 420-427. DOI: 10.1002/aic.690130308. (Companion to the Taylor-Aris dispersion theory; precursor to Whitaker, S. The Method of Volume Averaging, Kluwer, 1999.)
creator: Stephen Whitaker
prior_art_notes: Derives effective diffusion and hydrodynamic-dispersion coefficients in porous media by spatial volume averaging of the pointwise convection-diffusion equation - the porous-medium counterpart to Taylor-Aris dispersion in a single channel, and the basis for modelling transport in packed-bed microreactors, monolith columns, and porous-membrane microdevices. Discloses: the closure problem yielding the dispersion tensor in terms of pore-scale geometry; the dependence of longitudinal dispersion on Peclet number (transition from diffusion-dominated to mechanical-dispersion regimes); and the additive decomposition into effective molecular diffusion plus convective dispersion. Anticipates claims to dispersion-engineered porous microreactors, packed-bed-on-chip separation columns sized from volume-averaged coefficients, and porous-membrane microdevice transport models. Companion to taylor-aris-dispersion-1953 and aris-1956-dispersion-extension.
sources: Whitaker, S. The Method of Volume Averaging, Kluwer 1999
notes: Pre-1990; results unencumbered. Distinct from any existing Taylor-Aris entry; cross-referenced.

canonical_name: Fundamental Principles of Heat Transfer (Whitaker, 1977)
disclosure_citation: Whitaker, S. Fundamental Principles of Heat Transfer. Pergamon Press, 1977; reprinted Krieger, 1983. ISBN 0-08-017866-9.
creator: Stephen Whitaker
prior_art_notes: Graduate text deriving the convective-heat-transfer relations used to size microchannel heat exchangers, on-chip heaters, and PCR thermal cyclers. Discloses: the energy equation and its non-dimensionalisation (Peclet, Nusselt, Brinkman numbers); laminar forced convection in tubes and channels with worked solutions for constant-wall-temperature and constant-heat-flux boundary conditions (the Graetz problem, thermal entrance length, fully-developed Nusselt numbers); conjugate conduction-convection; and natural convection. The Whitaker correlation for forced-convection heat transfer over bodies is presented. Anticipates claims to thermal-entrance-length-corrected microchannel-cooler design and Graetz-problem-based on-chip thermal-cycler models. Companion to whitaker-1967-diffusion-dispersion-porous-media (same author) and tuckerman-pease-1981-microchannel-cooling.
sources: Whitaker, S. Fundamental Principles of Heat Transfer, Pergamon 1977; Krieger reprint 1983, ISBN 0-08-017866-9
notes: 1977 text; results unencumbered as prior art.

canonical_name: Acoustic frequency selection in microchannel ultrasonic standing-wave separation (Wiklund & Hertz, 2005)
disclosure_citation: Wiklund, M.; Hertz, H. M. Ultrasonic enhancement of bead-based bioaffinity assays. Lab Chip 2006, 6, 1279. Related: Wiklund, M.; Toivonen, J.; Tirri, M.; Hanninen, P.; Hertz, H. M. Ultrasonic enrichment of microspheres for ultrasensitive biomedical analysis in confocal laser-scanning fluorescence detection. J. Appl. Phys. 2004, 96, 1242. Hertz, H. M. Standing-wave acoustic trap for nonintrusive positioning of microparticles. J. Appl. Phys. 1995, 78, 4845.
creator: Martin Wiklund & Hans M. Hertz, KTH
prior_art_notes: Establishes how to choose the ultrasonic drive frequency for half-wavelength (and multi-node) standing-wave resonances in glass/silicon microchannels so that the acoustic radiation force concentrates particles or cells at pressure nodes - the design rule behind essentially all bulk-acoustic-wave acoustophoresis chips. Discloses: matching the channel width to an integer number of acoustic half-wavelengths in the fluid for a chosen transducer frequency; the resulting node positions and the dependence of trapping strength on frequency, channel resonance Q, and acoustic contrast factor; and integration of standing-wave trapping with confocal fluorescence detection for bead-based bioaffinity assays. Anticipates claims to frequency-tuned acoustophoretic microchannel separators, half-wavelength-resonator chip dimensioning, and acoustically enriched on-chip immunoassays. Companion to laurell-2007-acoustophoresis and the King 1934 / Yosioka-Kawasima 1955 / Gorkov 1962 acoustic-radiation-force lineage.
sources: Wiklund, M.; Hertz, H. M. Lab Chip 2006, 6, 1279
Wiklund, M. et al. J. Appl. Phys. 2004, 96, 1242
Hertz, H. M. J. Appl. Phys. 1995, 78, 4845
notes: Flagged in the wave-5 classical pass; the acoustic-frequency-selection thread. The 2005-era KTH work; engineering descriptions unencumbered as prior art.

canonical_name: Piezoresistance effect in germanium and silicon (C. S. Smith, 1954)
disclosure_citation: Smith, C. S. Piezoresistance effect in germanium and silicon. Phys. Rev. 1954, 94 (1), 42-49. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.94.42.
creator: Charles S. Smith (Case Institute / Bell Labs)
prior_art_notes: The foundational discovery that the electrical resistance of silicon and germanium changes strongly with mechanical strain (gauge factors ~100, two orders of magnitude larger than metal strain gauges), and that the effect is anisotropic with the largest longitudinal coefficient along <110> for p-type silicon. This is the physical basis of every integrated silicon pressure sensor and flow sensor used in microfluidic systems (diaphragm pressure transducers, thermal/pressure-drop flow meters, micropump back-pressure monitors). Discloses: the magnitude, sign, and crystallographic-orientation dependence of the piezoresistive coefficients of n- and p-type Si and Ge, and the recommended dopant types and orientations for maximum sensitivity. Anticipates claims to piezoresistive diaphragm pressure sensing in microfluidic chips, crystallographically-oriented strain gauges on micromachined membranes, and integrated flow-rate sensing via pressure-drop piezoresistors. Foundational ancestor of petersen-1982-silicon-mechanical-material and the silicon-micropump/microvalve lineage.
sources: Smith, C. S. Phys. Rev. 1954, 94, 42-49; DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.94.42
notes: 1954; public domain. Anchors the piezoresistive-sensing thread in the corpus.

canonical_name: Etched silicon vibrating (resonant) sensor (Greenwood, 1969)
disclosure_citation: Greenwood, J. C. Etched silicon vibrating sensor. (Early work on anisotropically etched single-crystal silicon resonant structures; later summarised in Greenwood, J. C. J. Phys. E: Sci. Instrum. 1984, 17, 650, and in Petersen, K. E. Proc. IEEE 1982, 70, 420.)
creator: J. C. Greenwood
prior_art_notes: Early demonstration that single-crystal silicon, anisotropically etched into thin beams/diaphragms, can be operated as a high-Q mechanical resonator whose frequency shifts with applied stress (pressure, force) or attached mass - the principle behind resonant silicon pressure sensors and, later, resonant-microchannel mass/density sensors used in microfluidics. Discloses: KOH-etched silicon beam/membrane resonators, electrostatic or piezoresistive drive/sense, and frequency-output (quasi-digital) transduction of pressure. Anticipates claims to resonant-mode pressure sensing integrated with microfluidic channels, stress-tuned silicon micro-resonators, and frequency-output flow/pressure sensors on chip. Cited by petersen-1982-silicon-mechanical-material.
sources: Greenwood, J. C., etched silicon vibrating sensor work, 1969 onward; J. Phys. E: Sci. Instrum. 1984, 17, 650
Petersen, K. E. Proc. IEEE 1982, 70, 420 (review citing this work)
notes: 1969 work; bibliographic detail thin for the earliest publication; included as a draft-quality lineage anchor for the resonant-silicon-sensor thread.

canonical_name: A gas chromatographic air analyzer fabricated on a silicon wafer (Terry, Jerman & Angell, 1979)
aliases: first integrated micro total analysis system
disclosure_citation: Terry, S. C.; Jerman, J. H.; Angell, J. B. A gas chromatographic air analyzer fabricated on a silicon wafer. IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 1979, 26 (12), 1880-1886. DOI: 10.1109/T-ED.1979.19791. (Based on Terry, S. C., PhD thesis, Stanford University, 1975.)
creator: Stephen C. Terry, J. Hal Jerman, James B. Angell, Stanford University
channel_geometry: 1.5 m spiral capillary column, ~200 um x 30 um cross-section, integrated on a 5 cm silicon wafer; integrated valve and thermal-conductivity detector
sensing: on-chip thermal-conductivity detector
prior_art_notes: The first integrated micro total analysis system (uTAS): a complete miniature gas chromatograph - sample-injection valve, 1.5-metre spiral separation column, and thermal-conductivity detector - photolithographically patterned and etched into a single silicon wafer with a glass cover, separating air mixtures in seconds. Discloses: a long spiral microchannel column anisotropically etched in silicon and sealed with a bonded glass lid; an integrated diaphragm sample-injection valve; an on-chip resistive thermal-conductivity detector; and the entire integrated-fabrication paradigm of putting a multi-component analytical instrument on a chip - the founding prior art for lab-on-a-chip. Anticipates claims to: spiral microchannel separation columns in silicon; monolithically integrated injector + column + detector; wafer-scale fabrication of a chemical analyzer; and the generic uTAS concept later named by Manz 1990. Distinct companion to the existing terry-1979-stanford-gas-chromatograph entry (this entry foregrounds the IEEE T-ED 26, 1880 publication and the uTAS-precedent framing); cross-referenced. Ancestor of manz-1990-mu-tas-concept and the entire lab-on-chip lineage.
sources: Terry, S. C.; Jerman, J. H.; Angell, J. B. IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 1979, 26, 1880-1886; DOI 10.1109/T-ED.1979.19791
Terry, S. C. A Gas Chromatography System Fabricated on a Silicon Wafer Using Integrated Circuit Technology. PhD thesis, Stanford University, 1975
notes: Distinct companion to existing terry-1979-stanford-gas-chromatograph. 1979 publication; public domain.

canonical_name: Ink jet printing nozzle arrays etched in (100) silicon (Bassous, Taub & Kuhn, 1977)
disclosure_citation: Bassous, E.; Taub, H. H.; Kuhn, L. Ink jet printing nozzle arrays etched in single-crystal silicon. Appl. Phys. Lett. 1977, 31 (2), 135-137. DOI: 10.1063/1.89587.
creator: Ernest Bassous, Harvey H. Taub, Larry Kuhn, IBM
channel_geometry: arrays of precisely sized orifices (tens of um) anisotropically etched through (100) silicon, defined by self-limiting {111}-bounded pyramidal pits
prior_art_notes: First demonstration of dimensionally precise micro-orifice arrays made by KOH anisotropic etching of (100) silicon for continuous-jet ink-jet printing - both a foundational MEMS fabrication result and a founding microfluidic-component disclosure. Discloses: square-mask anisotropic etching of (100) Si producing self-terminating {111}-walled pits and through-wafer orifices whose size is set photolithographically; arrays of such orifices on tight pitch with the uniformity needed for multi-nozzle ink jets; and the use of silicon micromachining to make a fluidic dispensing component. Anticipates claims to: silicon micromachined nozzle/orifice arrays; anisotropic-etch-defined microfluidic apertures; and wafer-scale fabrication of droplet-ejection arrays. Distinct companion to the existing bassous-1977-ibm-inkjet-nozzle entry (this entry foregrounds the Appl. Phys. Lett. 31, 135 disclosure and the array aspect); cross-referenced. Ancestor of the thermal- and piezoelectric-inkjet printheads (canon-bubble-jet-printhead, hp-thinkjet-thermal-inkjet) and of silicon-microfluidic fabrication generally.
sources: Bassous, E.; Taub, H. H.; Kuhn, L. Appl. Phys. Lett. 1977, 31, 135-137; DOI 10.1063/1.89587
notes: Distinct companion to existing bassous-1977-ibm-inkjet-nozzle. 1977; public domain.

canonical_name: Fabrication of novel three-dimensional microstructures by anisotropic etching of (100) and (110) silicon (Bassous, 1978)
disclosure_citation: Bassous, E. Fabrication of novel three-dimensional microstructures by the anisotropic etching of (100) and (110) silicon. IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 1978, 25 (10), 1178-1185. DOI: 10.1109/T-ED.1978.19250.
creator: Ernest Bassous, IBM
channel_geometry: V-grooves, pyramidal pits, through-holes, cantilevers, thin diaphragms and vertical-wall channels in (100) and (110) silicon defined by orientation-dependent KOH/EDP etching
prior_art_notes: The systematic exposition of how orientation-dependent (anisotropic) wet etching of (100) and (110) silicon produces a toolkit of three-dimensional microstructures: V-grooves, truncated pyramidal cavities, through-wafer holes, suspended diaphragms, cantilever beams, and - crucially for microfluidics - long channels with near-vertical (90 deg) walls in (110)-oriented wafers. Discloses: the {111}-stop self-limiting etch geometry; mask-to-feature transformation rules; thin-membrane and through-hole fabrication by timed/etch-stop methods; and the vertical-wall (110) channel that became a staple of early silicon microfluidic devices. Anticipates claims to: anisotropically-etched silicon microchannels with controlled wall angle; KOH-defined silicon diaphragms for pressure sensors and pump membranes; V-groove fiber/capillary alignment features; and through-wafer fluidic vias. Companion to bassous-taub-kuhn-1977-inkjet-nozzle-array-silicon (same author/era) and ancestor of petersen-1982-silicon-mechanical-material and the silicon-micropump/microvalve work (van-lintel-1988-silicon-piezo-pump, esashi-1989-silicon-piezo-pump).
sources: Bassous, E. IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 1978, 25, 1178-1185; DOI 10.1109/T-ED.1978.19250
notes: 1978; public domain.

canonical_name: Electrically activated normally-closed silicon diaphragm microvalves (Jerman, 1990)
disclosure_citation: Jerman, H. Electrically-activated, normally-closed diaphragm valves. Tech. Digest, Transducers 1991 (Int. Conf. Solid-State Sensors and Actuators), San Francisco, 1991, pp. 1045-1048. (Earlier presented at Transducers 1990; see also Jerman, H. J. Micromech. Microeng. 1994, 4, 210.) DOI: 10.1109/SENSOR.1991.149041.
creator: Hal Jerman, IC Sensors / EG&G IC Sensors
channel_geometry: bulk-micromachined silicon diaphragm valve seat with corrugated/flat membrane; flow ports ~ hundreds of um; thermopneumatic actuation cavity
prior_art_notes: A canonical early integrated silicon microvalve: a bulk-micromachined silicon diaphragm seals a valve seat in the normally-closed state and is lifted by thermopneumatic actuation (a sealed cavity of fluid heated by an integrated resistor expands and deflects the membrane) to open the flow path. Discloses: a normally-closed (fail-safe) micromachined valve architecture; thermopneumatic membrane actuation with an integrated heater; a micromachined valve seat and corrugated diaphragm for low leakage and large stroke; and integration of the valve with silicon flow channels. Anticipates claims to: normally-closed micromachined valves; thermopneumatic-actuated microfluidic valves; resistor-heated sealed-cavity membrane drives; and corrugated-diaphragm low-leakage valve seats. Companion to the silicon-micropump lineage (van-lintel-1988-silicon-piezo-pump, esashi-1989-silicon-piezo-pump, smits-1989-piezo-peristaltic-pump) and an ancestor of integrated microvalve technology preceding the Quake pneumatic-membrane valve (unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve).
notes: Presented Transducers 1990, published 1991; pre-1990s-microfluidics-patent-bulk treated as public-domain engineering disclosure.

canonical_name: A bidirectional silicon micropump (Zengerle, Richter, Sandmaier, 1992)
disclosure_citation: Zengerle, R.; Richter, A.; Sandmaier, H. A micro membrane pump with electrostatic actuation. Proc. IEEE Micro Electro Mechanical Systems (MEMS 1992), Travemunde, 1992, pp. 19-24. Zengerle, R.; Ulrich, J.; Kluge, S.; Richter, M.; Richter, A. A bidirectional silicon micropump. Sens. Actuators A 1995, 50, 81-86. DOI: 10.1016/0924-4247(96)80088-4.
creator: Roland Zengerle and coworkers, University of the German Armed Forces / IMM Mainz
channel_geometry: stacked silicon wafers forming a pump chamber with two passive check valves and an electrostatically actuated diaphragm; valve flaps and pump chamber at the hundreds-of-um scale
prior_art_notes: An electrostatically actuated silicon membrane micropump whose direction of net flow can be reversed by changing the actuation frequency, exploiting the frequency-dependent dynamics of its two passive flap check valves (above the resonance of one valve the pump runs forward, in a band between the two valve resonances it pumps backward). Discloses: an electrostatically driven pump diaphragm in stacked-silicon construction; two passive cantilever/flap check valves; and - the key result - bidirectional pumping from a single unidirectional-looking valve pair via valve-resonance-dependent rectification, plus self-priming and bubble-tolerant operation. Anticipates claims to: frequency-controlled flow reversal in passive-valve micropumps; electrostatic-membrane micropumps; and dual-check-valve rectifier pump architectures. Companion to van-lintel-1988-silicon-piezo-pump, esashi-1989-silicon-piezo-pump, and smits-1989-piezo-peristaltic-pump in the silicon-micropump lineage; the IMM Mainz pump that helped found integrated drug-delivery micropumps.
sources: Zengerle, R.; Richter, A.; Sandmaier, H. MEMS 1992, pp. 19-24
notes: 1992 MEMS conference; treated as public-domain engineering disclosure.

canonical_name: Microflow devices and systems (Shoji & Esashi review, 1994)
disclosure_citation: Shoji, S.; Esashi, M. Microflow devices and systems. J. Micromech. Microeng. 1994, 4 (4), 157-171. DOI: 10.1088/0960-1317/4/4/001.
creator: Shuichi Shoji & Masayoshi Esashi, Tohoku University
prior_art_notes: An early comprehensive review cataloguing the silicon-micromachined microfluidic component zoo as it stood in 1994 - micropumps (piezoelectric, electrostatic, thermopneumatic, peristaltic), microvalves (passive check valves, active normally-open and normally-closed valves), micro flow sensors, and integrated microflow systems including chemical analyzers - with comparative performance figures. Discloses, by reviewing the then-state-of-the-art, the design space of: diaphragm micropumps with passive flap valves; thermopneumatic and electrostatic membrane actuation; integrated silicon flow sensors (thermal and pressure-drop); and the integration of pumps, valves, sensors, and reaction chambers into microflow systems. Anticipates claims that would attempt to broadly cover micromachined-component microfluidic system architectures already surveyed here. Distinct companion to the existing esashi-1989-silicon-piezo-pump and gravesen-1993-microfluidics-review entries; cross-referenced. A bridging review between the 1970s-1980s silicon-MEMS era and the 1990s lab-on-chip explosion.
sources: Shoji, S.; Esashi, M. J. Micromech. Microeng. 1994, 4, 157-171; DOI 10.1088/0960-1317/4/4/001
notes: Distinct from existing esashi-1989-silicon-piezo-pump and gravesen-1993-microfluidics-review. 1994 review; engineering content unencumbered as prior art.

canonical_name: Micromachining a miniaturized capillary electrophoresis-based chemical analysis system on a chip (Harrison, Fluri, Seiler, Fan, Effenhauser, Manz, 1993)
disclosure_citation: Harrison, D. J.; Fluri, K.; Seiler, K.; Fan, Z.; Effenhauser, C. S.; Manz, A. Micromachining a miniaturized capillary electrophoresis-based chemical analysis system on a chip. Science 1993, 261 (5123), 895-897. DOI: 10.1126/science.261.5123.895.
creator: D. Jed Harrison (Alberta), Andreas Manz (Ciba-Geigy), and coworkers
channel_geometry: HF-etched glass channels ~30 um wide x ~10 um deep in a cross/double-T network with integrated reservoirs; chip a few cm across
sample_volume: sub-nL injected plug
sensing: on-chip laser-induced fluorescence
prior_art_notes: The landmark demonstration of an integrated capillary-electrophoresis chemical-analysis microchip - electrokinetically controlled sample handling, on-chip injection at a channel intersection, electrophoretic separation in HF-etched glass channels, and laser-induced-fluorescence detection - establishing the planar-glass uTAS platform that dominated the next decade. Discloses: a cross/double-T channel network with multiple reservoirs; voltage-program-controlled electrokinetic sample injection, separation, and dilution entirely by switching electrode potentials with no moving parts; sub-nL defined injection volumes; and integrated optical detection. Anticipates claims to: electrokinetically valved sample injection at channel intersections; multi-reservoir voltage-programmed CE microchips; HF-etched glass CE channel networks; and integrated LIF detection on a CE chip. Distinct companion to existing harrison-1992-cap-electrophoresis-on-chip and harrison-1993-electroosmotic-cycling entries; cross-referenced. Ancestor of jacobson-1994-pinched-injection, effenhauser-1993-glass-microchip-electrophoresis, mathies-1995-radial-cap-array, and burns-1998-integrated-dna-analysis-device.

Harrison, D. J.; Manz, A.; Fan, Z.; Ludi, H.; Widmer, H. M. Anal. Chem. 1992, 64, 1926 (the precursor)

canonical_name: Ultra-high-speed DNA fragment separations using microfabricated capillary array electrophoresis chips (Woolley & Mathies, 1994)
disclosure_citation: Woolley, A. T.; Mathies, R. A. Ultra-high-speed DNA fragment separations using microfabricated capillary array electrophoresis chips. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 1994, 91 (24), 11348-11352. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.91.24.11348.
creator: Adam T. Woolley & Richard A. Mathies, UC Berkeley
channel_geometry: HF-etched glass separation channels a few cm long, ~tens of um cross-section, loaded with sieving polymer; extended to multi-channel arrays
sensing: laser-induced fluorescence (later confocal scanner)
prior_art_notes: Demonstrated DNA-fragment electrophoretic separations on a glass microchip with a sieving polymer matrix achieving separations in seconds-to-minutes, and laid the groundwork for microfabricated capillary-array electrophoresis (CAE) for high-throughput DNA sizing and sequencing. Discloses: HF-etched glass channels filled with replaceable polymer sieving matrices for size separation of dsDNA; high-field ultra-fast electrophoresis enabled by efficient Joule-heat dissipation in shallow channels; on-chip LIF detection; and the scaling toward parallel channel arrays read by a scanning confocal detector. Anticipates claims to: polymer-sieving DNA separations in microchannels; high-field rapid microchip electrophoresis; capillary-array electrophoresis on a single substrate; and confocal-scanner readout of parallel separation channels. Distinct companion to existing mathies-1995-radial-cap-array; cross-referenced. Ancestor of microchip DNA-sequencing and high-throughput-genotyping platforms.

canonical_name: PCR in silicon microstructures (Wilding, Shoffner & Kricka, 1994)
disclosure_citation: Wilding, P.; Shoffner, M. A.; Kricka, L. J. PCR in a silicon microstructure. Clin. Chem. 1994, 40 (9), 1815-1818. DOI: 10.1093/clinchem/40.9.1815.
creator: Peter Wilding, Mann A. Shoffner, Larry J. Kricka, University of Pennsylvania
channel_geometry: anisotropically etched silicon reaction chamber (a few uL) sealed with a glass cover; surface-passivated walls
sensing: off-chip gel electrophoresis of product
prior_art_notes: One of the founding demonstrations of on-chip polymerase chain reaction: thermal cycling of a PCR mixture inside a silicon micromachined reaction chamber sealed with glass, with surface passivation to prevent inhibition of the polymerase by the silicon/oxide walls. Discloses: micromachined silicon-glass PCR chambers of microlitre volume; the wall-passivation problem (PCR inhibition by bare silicon, native oxide, and metals) and its mitigation by oxide growth, silanization, or BSA/polymer coating - a result essential to all subsequent on-chip PCR; rapid thermal cycling enabled by the small thermal mass; and successful amplification of human genomic targets in the chip. Anticipates claims to: micromachined PCR reaction chambers; surface-passivated silicon nucleic-acid-amplification cavities; small-thermal-mass rapid PCR cycling; and integration of PCR into a chip-scale diagnostic. Distinct from existing northrup-1993-silicon-pcr-microreactor (Lawrence Livermore device); cross-referenced as the parallel Penn origin. Ancestor of cheng-1996-chip-pcr-ii, continuous-flow PCR (kopp-1998-continuous-flow-pcr-on-chip), and integrated PCR-CE devices (burns-1998-integrated-dna-analysis-device).
sources: Wilding, P.; Shoffner, M. A.; Kricka, L. J. Clin. Chem. 1994, 40, 1815-1818; DOI 10.1093/clinchem/40.9.1815
Shoffner, M. A. et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 1996, 24, 375; Cheng, J. et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 1996, 24, 380
notes: Distinct from existing northrup-1993-silicon-pcr-microreactor. 1994; treated as public-domain engineering disclosure.

canonical_name: Chemical amplification: continuous-flow PCR on a chip (Kopp, de Mello & Manz, 1998)
disclosure_citation: Kopp, M. U.; de Mello, A. J.; Manz, A. Chemical amplification: continuous-flow PCR on a chip. Science 1998, 280 (5366), 1046-1048. DOI: 10.1126/science.280.5366.1046.
creator: Martin U. Kopp, Andrew J. de Mello, Andreas Manz, Imperial College London
channel_geometry: serpentine glass microchannel (~tens of um cross-section) routed repeatedly across three fixed temperature zones; 20 cycles in a single pass; chip a few cm across
sample_volume: continuous flow, nL-scale residence per zone
throughput: as fast as ~90 s for 20 cycles at high flow rate
sensing: off-chip gel/CE analysis of product
prior_art_notes: Introduced continuous-flow (flow-through) PCR: instead of cycling the temperature of a static chamber, the reaction mixture is pumped through a serpentine microchannel that repeatedly traverses three zones held at fixed denaturation, annealing, and extension temperatures, so the time-domain thermal protocol becomes a spatial one - removing thermal-ramp limits and enabling very fast amplification. Discloses: spatially-multiplexed isothermal-zone architecture for thermal cycling; cycle number set by channel geometry (number of passes); cycle time set by flow rate and zone-segment lengths; and the elimination of bulk-heater thermal mass as the rate limit. Anticipates claims to: continuous-flow / flow-through nucleic-acid amplification microdevices; fixed-temperature-zone serpentine PCR chips; flow-rate-controlled cycling kinetics; and spatial-domain implementations of any cyclic thermal protocol. Companion to wilding-shoffner-kricka-1994-pcr-in-silicon-microstructures and northrup-1993-silicon-pcr-microreactor (static-chamber predecessors); ancestor of droplet-PCR and microfluidic digital-PCR throughput architectures.
sources: Kopp, M. U.; de Mello, A. J.; Manz, A. Science 1998, 280, 1046-1048; DOI 10.1126/science.280.5366.1046
notes: 1998; treated as public-domain engineering disclosure.

canonical_name: A nanoliter-scale nucleic acid processor with parallel architecture (Hong, Studer, Hang, Anderson, Quake, 2004)
disclosure_citation: Hong, J. W.; Studer, V.; Hang, G.; Anderson, W. F.; Quake, S. R. A nanoliter-scale nucleic acid processor with parallel architecture. Nat. Biotechnol. 2004, 22 (4), 435-439. DOI: 10.1038/nbt951.
creator: Jong Wook Hong, Vincent Studer, Stephen R. Quake, Caltech
channel_geometry: multilayer-soft-lithography PDMS chip with hundreds of pneumatic membrane valves defining parallel nL reaction units; flow channels ~100 um, valve control lines crossing above
sample_volume: tens of nL per reactor
throughput: parallel processing of multiple samples on one chip
sensing: off-chip / fluorescence
prior_art_notes: An integrated PDMS lab-on-a-chip that performs the full nucleic-acid-preparation workflow - cell isolation, lysis, mRNA/DNA capture on functionalized beads, washing, and recovery of purified product - in parallel nanolitre reactors, built entirely from multilayer-soft-lithography pneumatic membrane valves and peristaltic pumps. Discloses: a parallel-architecture chip in which dozens of membrane valves partition and route fluids among rotary mixers, bead-capture columns, and elution channels; on-chip affinity capture (paramagnetic or affinity beads trapped behind a sieve valve) for solid-phase nucleic-acid purification; on-chip peristaltic metering and rotary mixing; and recovery of purified mRNA/DNA from single-cell-quantity inputs. Anticipates claims to: integrated multi-step nucleic-acid sample preparation in valve-controlled PDMS chips; parallelized nL bead-based extraction columns on chip; rotary-mixer reaction units fed by membrane-valve manifolds; and single-cell nucleic-acid processing pipelines. Builds on unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve and thorsen-2002-microfluidic-large-scale-integration; commercialized via Fluidigm.
sources: Hong, J. W.; Studer, V.; Hang, G.; Anderson, W. F.; Quake, S. R. Nat. Biotechnol. 2004, 22, 435-439; DOI 10.1038/nbt951
notes: MLSI / Fluidigm lineage; patented. Cross-reference: unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve, thorsen-2002-microfluidic-large-scale-integration.

canonical_name: Soft lithography for micro- and nanoscale patterning (Qin, Xia & Whitesides, Nature Protocols, 2010)
disclosure_citation: Qin, D.; Xia, Y.; Whitesides, G. M. Soft lithography for micro- and nanoscale patterning. Nat. Protoc. 2010, 5 (3), 491-502. DOI: 10.1038/nprot.2009.234.
creator: Dong Qin, Younan Xia, George M. Whitesides, Harvard
channel_geometry: step-by-step protocol for SU-8 master mask design (down to ~1-10 um features), PDMS casting and curing, plasma bonding to glass/PDMS, and port punching
prior_art_notes: The widely-followed step-by-step protocol that codified PDMS soft-lithography microfabrication for non-specialist laboratories - the de facto foundry recipe behind a large fraction of academic microfluidic devices. Discloses, in reproducible detail: photomask layout and printing; SU-8 photoresist master fabrication on silicon with feature heights from a few microns to hundreds of microns; degassed-PDMS casting, curing, and demolding; oxygen-plasma activation and irreversible PDMS-glass and PDMS-PDMS bonding; inlet/outlet punching and tubing interfacing; and multilayer alignment for valve chips. Anticipates claims to: standardized PDMS replica-molding microfluidic fabrication workflows; plasma-bonded PDMS-glass channel sealing; SU-8-master-defined microchannel geometries; and the generic rapid-prototyping foundry process. Distinct from existing duffy-1998-pdms-soft-lithography-microfluidics, xia-whitesides-1998-soft-lithography-review, mcdonald-whitesides-2002-pdms-review, and whitesides-2010-mu-pads-systematic; cross-referenced as the published protocol node of the Whitesides soft-lithography lineage (the patented aspects are covered by whitesides-patent-family-soft-lithography).

disclosure_citation: Margulies et al., Genome sequencing in microfabricated high-density picolitre reactors, Nature 437, 376-380 (2005). DOI: 10.1038/nature03959. Roche acquired 454 Life Sciences 2007 (CuraGen sale); Roche acquired Genia Technologies 2014-06-02 (~US 125M + milestones).

Roche shut down the 454 platform in 2013 after Illumina out-competed it on cost. The picotiter-plate well-array and the emulsion-PCR bead workflow are direct ancestors of Ion Torrent (rothberg-2011-ion-torrent, already in corpus) and of all subsequent bead-in-droplet clonal-amplification platforms. Genia CMOS-integrated, electrically-addressed nanopore array (acquired 2014) is prior art for solid-state and protein-nanopore sensor arrays, relevant to clarke-2009-nanopore-sequencing and oxford-nanopore-minion. canonical_name: Complete Genomics DNA-nanoball sequencing patent estate (acquired by BGI 2013)
channel_geometry: patterned silicon flow-slide: ordered array of ~300 nm spots on a sub-um grid pitch, each binding one ~200 nm DNA nanoball
creator: Complete Genomics, Inc. (founded 2006; acquired by BGI-Shenzhen 2013; now MGI Tech)
disclosure_citation: Drmanac et al., Human genome sequencing using unchained base reads on self-assembling DNA nanoarrays, Science 327, 78-81 (2010). DOI: 10.1126/science.1181498. BGI completed acquisition of Complete Genomics 2013-03-18 (Complete Genomics 8-K / DEFM14A; ~US 117.6M).

notes: Wave 6. The basis of BGI/MGI DNBSEQ; the subject of Illumina v. Complete Genomics.

The patterned-array flow-slide and the DNB chemistry are the technical basis of MGI DNBSEQ instruments (DNBSEQ-G400, -T7, -G99) sold worldwide today. Prior art for patterned-flowcell ordered-array sequencing, directly relevant to Illumina patterned flowcell descendants of bentley-2008-illumina-flow-cell and to Element AVITI avidity sequencing. The CGI estate is the IP Illumina tried to block via litigation before BGI acquisition (see illumina-vs-complete-genomics-litigation).

canonical_name: Illumina acquisition of Solexa 2007 (sequencing-by-synthesis IP; Solexa/Manteia/Lynx Therapeutics chain)

creator: Illumina, Inc. (acquirer); Solexa, Inc./Ltd. (target; built on Manteia SA and Lynx Therapeutics IP)
disclosure_citation: Illumina, Inc. acquisition of Solexa, Inc. completed 2007-01-26 (Illumina 8-K 2007-01-26; ~US 650M stock). Underlying technology: Bentley et al., Accurate whole human genome sequencing using reversible terminator chemistry, Nature 456, 53-59 (2008). DOI: 10.1038/nature07517.

This is the foundational IP behind every Illumina sequencer (GA, HiSeq, MiSeq, NextSeq, NovaSeq) and the most-litigated estate in genomics (BGI, Oxford Nanopore, Complete Genomics, QIAGEN/Intelligent Bio Solutions). Original Solexa cluster/bridge-amplification patents began expiring ~2018-2023; the corpus records the chain so post-expiry SBS-on-patterned-flowcell claims are anticipated. Lineage child of lynx-therapeutics-mpss and manteia-sa-bridge-amplification (this wave); descendant chains include bentley-2008-illumina-flow-cell.

canonical_name: Lynx Therapeutics MPSS (massively parallel signature sequencing) bead-array patents
channel_geometry: flow cell packed with a planar monolayer of ~1.6 million 5 um microbeads, each bearing ~10^5 copies of one cloned cDNA fragment
creator: Lynx Therapeutics, Inc. (Hayward, CA; spun out of Applied Biosystems 1992; merged with Solexa 2005)
disclosure_citation: Brenner et al., Gene expression analysis by massively parallel signature sequencing (MPSS) on microbead arrays, Nature Biotechnology 18, 630-634 (2000). DOI: 10.1038/76469. Earlier: Brenner and Lerner, Encoded combinatorial chemistry, PNAS 89, 5381-5383 (1992).

notes: Wave 6. The pre-Solexa bead-array origin of massively-parallel sequencing.
prior_art_notes: Lynx MPSS was the first true massively-parallel sequencing platform: in vitro clonal amplification of a tagged cDNA library onto microbeads, hybridization-based bead sorting by anti-tag, packing of the bead monolayer into a flow cell, and cyclic ligation-based readout of short signature sequences from each bead. The microbead-monolayer flow cell, the clonal one-fragment-per-bead amplification, and the cyclic ligation chemistry are all ancestors of 454 emulsion-PCR beads, SOLiD bead arrays, Ion Torrent, and (via the Solexa merger) Illumina clusters. Brenner oligonucleotide-tag patents (US 5,604,097 etc.) are foundational prior art for combinatorial barcoding, sample multiplexing, and unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), relevant to macosko-2015-drop-seq, klein-2015-indrops, and every single-cell barcoding scheme. Patents from the 1990s; mostly expired by ~2014-2017, now public domain.
sample_volume: microliter cyclic reagent exchange over a bead monolayer
throughput: ~10^6 distinct 17-20 bp signature reads per run (then unprecedented)

canonical_name: Manteia SA solid-phase bridge-amplification patents (Geneva)
channel_geometry: planar glass surface grafted with a dense lawn of two oligonucleotide primers; isothermal bridge PCR forms ~1 um clonal clusters (DNA colonies) at ~10^7-10^8 per cm^2
creator: Manteia SA (Coinsins/Geneva, Switzerland; technology licensed to Solexa 2004)
disclosure_citation: Mayer, Kawashima et al., Method of nucleic acid amplification, WO 98/44151 / EP 0,985,142 B1 (priority 1997-04-01); US 7,115,400. Characterisation: Adessi et al., Solid phase DNA amplification, Nucleic Acids Research 28, e87 (2000). DOI: 10.1093/nar/28.20.e87.
ip_citations: EP 0,985,142 B1 (Mayer/Kawashima, Method of nucleic acid amplification, priority 1997)
notes: Wave 6. The Geneva origin of Illumina cluster amplification.
prior_art_notes: Manteia SA invented solid-phase bridge amplification: a planar surface is grafted with a lawn of two primer oligos; a single template molecule hybridizes, extends, then bends over (bridges) to the adjacent surface primer, and isothermal cycling produces a clonal cluster of ~1000 copies anchored to a ~1 um patch of surface. This is the cluster-generation chemistry at the heart of every Illumina flowcell. Solexa licensed it from Manteia in 2004; Illumina acquired Solexa (and the licensed Manteia rights) in 2007. The Manteia priority date (April 1997) is the earliest critical date for solid-phase clonal-cluster amplification, prior art against any later clusters-on-a-surface or polony claim. Closely related to and roughly contemporaneous with Mitra and Church polony (polymerase colony) work; the corpus records both to map the surface-clonal-amplification prior art landscape. Anticipates: bentley-2008-illumina-flow-cell, Complete Genomics patterned arrays, Element AVITI surface chemistry.
sample_volume: microliter reagent exchange over a planar grafted surface
sources: Fedurco et al. 2006 NAR 34:e22 (BTA reagent for DNA attachment on glass)

disclosure_citation: Skeggs, An automatic method for colorimetric analysis, American Journal of Clinical Pathology 28, 311-322 (1957) (the Technicon AutoAnalyzer continuous-flow segmented-flow analysis principle). Bayer acquired Chiron Diagnostics 1998; Siemens acquired Bayer Diagnostics 2007.

notes: Wave 6. The Technicon segmented-flow origin matters: pre-microfluidics droplet-in-tube prior art.
prior_art_notes: The Technicon AutoAnalyzer (Skeggs, 1957) introduced air-segmented continuous-flow analysis, dividing a reagent stream into discrete liquid plugs separated by air bubbles flowing through narrow tubing, which is the conceptual ancestor of segmented-flow and droplet microfluidics for chemical analysis (decades before microfluidics as a term, and before Manz micro-TAS). Skeggs segmented-flow patents are long expired; the air-bubble-plug analysis principle is public domain prior art for any segmented-flow assay claim, including modern droplet ddPCR plug-flow concepts. The Chiron/ADVIA Centaur acridinium-ester chemiluminescent immunoassay automation is prior art for automated bead-based immunoassay sample handling. This estate was absorbed by Bayer (1998 Chiron Diagnostics deal) and then Siemens (2007).

prior_art_notes: Sysmex (as Toa Medical Electronics) commercialized hydrodynamically-focused sheath-flow cytometry for routine hematology from the 1980s onward, decades before the term microfluidics. Many of the foundational Toa/Sysmex sheath-flow patents from the 1980s-90s have expired and are now European/Japanese public-domain prior art. Extends wave 5 Sysmex entry; emphasizes the European-grandfathered hematology IP that pre-dates academic microfluidics by ~15 years.

notes: Wave 6 landmark litigation. The Section 101 case that struck the foundational NIPT patent.
prior_art_notes: The most cited diagnostics Section 101 case after Mayo and Myriad. Sequenom US 6,258,540 covered the foundational insight (Lo et al. 1997) that cell-free fetal DNA circulates in maternal plasma and can be amplified and detected non-invasively - the basis of all non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). The Federal Circuit (788 F.3d 1371, 2015) held the claims patent-ineligible: the natural phenomenon (cffDNA in maternal plasma) plus only conventional amplification/detection steps was not significantly more under the Mayo/Alice framework. En banc rehearing was denied over notable concurrences lamenting the result, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 2016. The practical effect: NIPT became a crowded competitive field (Sequenom, Illumina/Verinata, Ariosa/Roche, Natera, etc.) because the gatekeeping method patent fell. For this corpus, the case is the canonical demonstration that disclosing a microfluidic/molecular diagnostic method that merely applies routine PCR/sequencing to a natural correlation does not yield enforceable claims - the device implementation, not the discovered correlation, is where defensible IP (and useful prior art) lives.
