throughput: time-domain thermal cycling by convecting fluid past fixed heaters; full PCR in tens of minutes
sensing: on-chip / off-chip fluorescence of product
notable_capabilities: rotary closed-loop reaction channel with integrated peristaltic micropump
thermal cycling by pumping liquid past three fixed-temperature zones
Quake-style monolithic membrane (MLSI) valves and pumps
nanoliter PCR with no moving fluid interfaces and reduced evaporation
prior_art_notes: Discloses the rotary PCR architecture: a closed-loop nanoliter channel in PDMS with three integrated peristaltic Quake (MLSI) micropumps that convect the reaction mixture around a circuit passing three fixed-temperature zones - thermal cycling in the spatial domain at constant heater temperatures, avoiding the thermal mass and ramp limits of cycling the whole chip. Anticipates claims to: continuous-flow PCR in a recirculating loop driven by an on-chip pump; spatial-domain thermal cycling by transporting reagent past stationary heaters; integration of a closed-loop reactor with monolithic pneumatic peristaltic pumping; and nanoliter-scale recirculating reaction networks generally. Foundational for later continuous-flow / recirculating-loop PCR chips and droplet-recirculation reactors. Quake-lab MLSI lineage (unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve).
notes: Quake lab MLSI series. Distinct from liu-2002-paraffin-thermal-valve (different Liu 2002 on paraffin valves). The seminal recirculating-loop PCR architecture.

canonical_name: Studer 2004 scaling properties of a low-actuation-pressure microfluidic valve
disclosure_citation: Studer, V.; Hang, G.; Pandolfi, A.; Ortiz, M.; Anderson, W. F.; Quake, S. R. Scaling properties of a low-actuation-pressure microfluidic valve. J. Appl. Phys. 2004, 95, 393-398. DOI: 10.1063/1.1629781
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Caltech
channel_geometry: push-up monolithic PDMS membrane valve; rounded flow channel cross-section; valve closure modeled vs membrane thickness, channel width, applied pressure
notable_capabilities: push-up valve geometry with sub-1-psi closure pressure
analytic + finite-element scaling model of membrane-valve closure
design rules relating membrane thickness, channel dimensions and actuation pressure
enables dense valve arrays with low-pressure manifolds
prior_art_notes: Establishes the quantitative design rules for monolithic-membrane (Quake/MLSI) microvalves and introduces the push-up valve geometry that achieves valve closure at sub-1-psi actuation pressures. Discloses: the mechanical model (membrane bending, contact mechanics) relating closure pressure to membrane thickness and channel width; the push-up vs push-down configuration trade-off; and the scaling that makes large valve arrays driven by modest pressure feasible. Anticipates claims to: low-actuation-pressure elastomeric membrane valves; push-up valve geometry; and parametric design methodologies for membrane-deflection microvalves. Core reference for the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry MLSI design-rule documents (cf. hong-studer-quake-2004-nanoliter-nucleic-acid-processor, unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve).
notes: Quake lab MLSI design-rules series; companion to unger-2000-quake-monolithic-membrane-valve and the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry design rules.

canonical_name: Hong and Quake 2003 integrated nanoliter systems
disclosure_citation: Hong, J. W.; Quake, S. R. Integrated nanoliter systems. Nat. Biotechnol. 2003, 21, 1179-1183. DOI: 10.1038/nbt871
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Caltech
notable_capabilities: survey of microfluidic large-scale integration (MLSI) for nanoliter biochemistry
multiplexer addressing of N channels with ~log2(N) control lines
peristaltic pumps, mixers, rotary reactors, microcolumns from monolithic valves
blueprint for the chip-scale automation that became the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry / Fluidigm platform
prior_art_notes: The canonical mid-period statement of microfluidic large-scale integration: assembling thousands of monolithic-membrane valves into multiplexers, peristaltic pumps, rotary mixers, on-chip columns and addressable chamber arrays for nanoliter-scale biochemistry and genomics. Discloses (in a unified review form) the multiplexer scheme that addresses N independent fluidic lines with order log2(N) control inputs, the integration of metering/mixing/incubation/separation modules on a single PDMS chip, and the architecture later commercialized as the Fluidigm dynamic-array / Stanford Microfluidics Foundry platform (cf. fluidigm-patent-family-biomark-dynamic-array, quake-patent-family-mlsi-monolithic-membrane-valve). Anticipates claims to: combinatorial multiplexer addressing of valve arrays; integrated nanoliter reaction-array chips; and chip-scale automation of multi-step biochemical workflows.
notes: Distinct from hong-studer-quake-2004-nanoliter-nucleic-acid-processor (the 2004 device paper). This is the 2003 review that named and codified the Stanford foundry / Fluidigm architecture.

canonical_name: Hansen 2002 robust scalable microfluidic metering for protein crystallization by free interface diffusion
disclosure_citation: Hansen, C. L.; Skordalakes, E.; Berger, J. M.; Quake, S. R. A robust and scalable microfluidic metering method that allows protein crystal growth by free interface diffusion. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 2002, 99, 16531-16536. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.262485199
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Caltech
channel_geometry: arrays of paired nanoliter chambers separated by an interface valve; valve opened to allow free-interface diffusion between protein and precipitant; hundreds of conditions per chip
sample_volume: few nL per crystallization trial
throughput: hundreds of crystallization conditions per chip from microliter-scale protein stock
notable_capabilities: dead-volume-free metering of paired nanoliter aliquots via monolithic valves
free-interface-diffusion crystallization (impossible to do reproducibly by hand at this scale)
massively parallel screening of crystallization phase space from tiny protein amounts
commercialized as the Fluidigm Topaz crystallization system
prior_art_notes: Discloses the microfluidic metering method underlying chip-format protein crystallization: paired nanoliter chambers loaded by dead-end filling, isolated by monolithic membrane valves, then connected through an interface valve so the two reagents mix only by free-interface diffusion - reproducibly sampling a crystallization trajectory through supersaturation space that is impractical to set up by hand at nanoliter scale. Anticipates claims to: dead-volume-free metering of defined nanoliter aliquots by valve-bounded chamber filling; free-interface-diffusion crystallization in a microfluidic chamber array; and high-throughput crystallization screening from microgram protein quantities. Commercialized as Fluidigm Topaz. Companion to quake-2003-microfluidic-protein-crystallization. Quake-lab MLSI lineage.
notes: Companion to quake-2003-microfluidic-protein-crystallization (Hansen Quake 2003). This is the foundational 2002 PNAS metering paper; basis of the Fluidigm Topaz product.

canonical_name: Marcus 2006 microfluidic single-cell mRNA isolation and analysis
disclosure_citation: Marcus, J. S.; Anderson, W. F.; Quake, S. R. Microfluidic single-cell mRNA isolation and analysis. Anal. Chem. 2006, 78, 3084-3089. DOI: 10.1021/ac0519460
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Caltech
channel_geometry: multilayer PDMS chip with isolated nanoliter processing chambers, monolithic valves, oligo-dT-bead affinity column; pipeline: cell capture -> lysis -> mRNA capture -> wash -> cDNA elution
sample_volume: single cell; nanoliter chambers
throughput: parallel single-cell processing lanes
sensing: downstream qPCR of recovered cDNA
notable_capabilities: capture and lysis of an individual cell in an isolated nanoliter chamber
on-chip oligo-dT affinity capture and purification of single-cell mRNA
on-chip reverse transcription / cDNA recovery
one of the first end-to-end single-cell transcriptomic sample-prep chips
prior_art_notes: An early end-to-end single-cell mRNA sample-preparation chip: a multilayer PDMS device that captures one cell in an isolated nanoliter chamber, lyses it, captures the released mRNA on an oligo-dT affinity bead column, washes, and reverse-transcribes / elutes cDNA for downstream qPCR - all with monolithic membrane valves and dead-volume-controlled metering. Anticipates claims to: isolation of a single cell in a valve-bounded nanoliter reaction chamber for nucleic-acid extraction; on-chip oligo-dT affinity capture of polyadenylated RNA from a single-cell lysate; and integrated single-cell lysis + RNA purification + reverse transcription in one microfluidic device. Conceptual ancestor of later single-cell RNA-seq sample-prep chips (Fluidigm C1 and droplet scRNA-seq). Quake-lab MLSI lineage.
notes: Quake lab MLSI single-cell series; ancestor of the Fluidigm C1 single-cell platform.

canonical_name: Maerkl and Quake 2007 systems approach to measuring transcription-factor binding energy landscapes (MITOMI)
aliases: mechanically induced trapping of molecular interactions
disclosure_citation: Maerkl, S. J.; Quake, S. R. A systems approach to measuring the binding energy landscapes of transcription factors. Science 2007, 315, 233-237. DOI: 10.1126/science.1131007
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Stanford / Caltech
channel_geometry: two-layer PDMS chip with ~2400 unit cells; each cell has a chamber, a button membrane that mechanically traps surface-bound complexes, DNA-spotting region, and monolithic isolation valves
sample_volume: sub-nL per unit cell
throughput: ~2400 simultaneous equilibrium binding measurements per chip
sensing: surface fluorescence quantitation under the button valve
notable_capabilities: mechanically induced trapping of molecular interactions (MITOMI) via a button membrane valve
thousands of in-vitro equilibrium binding assays in parallel from on-chip-synthesized protein
full binding-energy landscape (every DNA k-mer) for a transcription factor on one chip
general platform for high-throughput protein-DNA / protein-ligand affinity measurement
prior_art_notes: Discloses the MITOMI architecture: a dense array of PDMS unit cells where a circular button membrane valve is lowered onto a functionalized surface to mechanically trap surface-bound molecular complexes at the instant of measurement, defeating dissociation during washing and enabling thousands of true equilibrium-affinity measurements in parallel - here used to map the complete binding-energy landscape of transcription factors against every DNA sequence variant. Anticipates claims to: a button/doormat membrane valve used to capture and protect a surface-immobilized binding complex during washout; massively parallel on-chip equilibrium binding-constant arrays with in-situ-expressed protein; and microfluidic measurement of full sequence-resolved binding landscapes. The MITOMI button-valve trick is widely reused; this is its origin. Quake-lab MLSI lineage.
notes: Quake lab MLSI series. Origin of the MITOMI button-valve molecular-trapping technique.

canonical_name: Melin and Quake 2007 microfluidic large-scale integration: evolution of design rules for biological automation
disclosure_citation: Melin, J.; Quake, S. R. Microfluidic large-scale integration: the evolution of design rules for biological automation. Annu. Rev. Biophys. Biomol. Struct. 2007, 36, 213-231. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.biophys.36.040306.132646
creator: Stephen R. Quake group, Stanford
notable_capabilities: codification of MLSI design rules (valve pitch, multiplexer fan-out, channel rounding, push-up vs push-down)
analogy to integrated-circuit design-rule scaling
catalog of MLSI primitives: valves, pumps, multiplexers, mixers, micro-columns, cell traps, MITOMI buttons
reference text for the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry
prior_art_notes: The review that explicitly frames microfluidic large-scale integration as having design rules analogous to VLSI: minimum valve dimensions, multiplexer fan-out limits, channel-rounding requirements, push-up vs push-down valve choices, manifold pressure budgets, and the composition rules for assembling valves into pumps, mixers, rotary reactors, micro-columns, addressable chamber arrays, cell traps and MITOMI button cells. As a unified prior-art statement it anticipates claims to: parametric/rule-based design methodologies for elastomeric valve arrays; the standard MLSI primitive library; and software-assisted layout of multilayer soft-lithography chips. Core reference document for the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry (companion to hong-quake-2003-integrated-nanoliter-systems and studer-2004-low-actuation-pressure-microfluidic-valve).
notes: Quake lab. The design-rules review for the Stanford Microfluidics Foundry / MLSI ecosystem.

canonical_name: Whitesides 2001 soft lithography in biology and biochemistry
disclosure_citation: Whitesides, G. M.; Ostuni, E.; Takayama, S.; Jiang, X.; Ingber, D. E. Soft lithography in biology and biochemistry. Annu. Rev. Biomed. Eng. 2001, 3, 335-373. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.bioeng.3.1.335
creator: George M. Whitesides group, Harvard (with Ingber, Wyss precursor)
notable_capabilities: catalog of soft-lithographic techniques for biology: microcontact printing, replica molding, microfluidic patterning, stencils, laminar-flow patterning
patterning cells, proteins, ECM on surfaces with micrometer control
laminar co-flow used to deliver reagents to subcellular regions of a single cell
foundational methods review for PDMS microfluidics in cell biology
prior_art_notes: The canonical review of soft lithography applied to cell biology and biochemistry: microcontact printing of self-assembled monolayers, replica molding of PDMS, microfluidic and stencil patterning of cells and proteins, laminar-flow (multi-stream) patterning to address subcellular regions, and the use of these to build patterned co-cultures and surface gradients. As prior art it anticipates claims to: patterning adherent cells or biomolecules on a substrate by PDMS stamp / stencil / microfluidic channel; laminar co-flow delivery of distinct fluids to selected portions of a cell or surface; and the general toolkit of PDMS-based bio-patterning. Companion to xia-whitesides-1998-soft-lithography-review and the Ingber organ-chip lineage (huh-2010-lung-on-chip). One of the most-cited microfluidics-in-biology references.
notes: Whitesides/Ingber. Foundational soft-lithography-in-biology review; conceptual ancestor of organ-on-chip work.

canonical_name: Sia and Whitesides 2003 microfluidic devices fabricated in PDMS for biological studies
disclosure_citation: Sia, S. K.; Whitesides, G. M. Microfluidic devices fabricated in poly(dimethylsiloxane) for biological studies. Electrophoresis 2003, 24, 3563-3576. DOI: 10.1002/elps.200305584
creator: George M. Whitesides group, Harvard
notable_capabilities: practical review of PDMS microfluidics for biology: fabrication, surface treatment, bonding, world-to-chip interconnects
catalog of biological applications: immunoassays, cell handling, protein crystallization, patterning, gradient generators
discussion of PDMS limitations (small-molecule absorption, permeability, swelling)
standard how-to reference adopted across the field
prior_art_notes: The practical handbook-style review of PDMS microfluidics for biology: rapid prototyping by soft lithography, plasma bonding, world-to-chip interconnects, surface modification and passivation strategies, and a catalog of biological uses (heterogeneous immunoassays, cell capture and culture, on-chip protein crystallization, surface and solution-gradient generators) plus a frank treatment of PDMS limitations. As prior art it anticipates claims to: standard PDMS device fabrication and bonding workflows; common PDMS-chip surface-treatment recipes for biocompatibility; and the general designs of PDMS gradient generators and cell-handling chips. Companion to mcdonald-whitesides-2002-pdms-review and whitesides-2001-soft-lithography-in-biology.
notes: Whitesides lab. Practical PDMS-microfluidics-for-biology review; widely cited methods reference.

canonical_name: Garstecki 2006 formation of droplets and bubbles in a microfluidic T-junction
disclosure_citation: Garstecki, P.; Fuerstman, M. J.; Stone, H. A.; Whitesides, G. M. Formation of droplets and bubbles in a microfluidic T-junction - scaling and mechanism of break-up. Lab Chip 2006, 6, 437-446. DOI: 10.1039/b510841a
creator: Whitesides / Stone groups, Harvard
channel_geometry: cross/T-junction of a dispersed-phase side channel into a continuous-phase main channel; rectangular microchannels; squeezing-regime break-up at low capillary number
throughput: droplet size set by flow-rate ratio; high monodispersity
notable_capabilities: squeezing-regime model of T-junction break-up: droplet length = 1 + alpha*(Q_disp/Q_cont)
break-up dominated by pressure buildup, not shear, at low Ca
predictive design rule for T-junction droplet/bubble length
applies to both liquid droplets and gas bubbles
prior_art_notes: The anchor reference for T-junction droplet generation: it identifies the squeezing regime in which the dispersed phase obstructs the main channel and break-up is driven by the upstream pressure rise rather than by viscous shear, and derives the linear scaling droplet-length = 1 + alpha*(flow-rate ratio) that has become the standard T-junction design rule. As prior art it anticipates claims to: generating monodisperse droplets or bubbles at a T-/cross-junction with size set by the flow-rate ratio in the squeezing regime; and design methods predicting droplet length from junction geometry and flow ratio. Companion to thorsen-2002-droplet-microfluidics-flow-focusing and anna-2003-flow-focusing-droplet; with them it defines the canonical droplet-generator geometries. Whitesides/Stone droplet lineage.
notes: Whitesides/Stone. The T-junction droplet anchor; standard squeezing-regime design rule.

canonical_name: Tan 2004 design of microfluidic channel geometries for control of droplet volume
disclosure_citation: Tan, Y.-C.; Fisher, J. S.; Lee, A. I.; Cristini, V.; Lee, A. P. Design of microfluidic channel geometries for the control of droplet volume, chemical concentration, and sorting. Lab Chip 2004, 4, 292-298. DOI: 10.1039/b403280m
creator: Abraham P. Lee group, UC Irvine (with Cristini, UCI math)
channel_geometry: flow-focusing droplet generator with downstream expansion/contraction and bifurcating channels; passive break-up of mother droplets into controlled daughter volumes; geometry-defined sorting at bifurcations
throughput: on-the-fly tuning of droplet volume and concentration via channel geometry
notable_capabilities: passive splitting of droplets at channel bifurcations into prescribed volume ratios
downstream geometry (expansion, branching) used to set final droplet size from a single generator
passive size-based sorting of droplets at asymmetric bifurcations
on-chip dilution series by serial droplet splitting
prior_art_notes: Discloses use of downstream channel geometry (expansions, contractions, T- and Y-bifurcations) to passively control droplet volume, to split a mother droplet into daughter droplets of designed volume ratio, to build on-chip dilution series, and to sort droplets by size at asymmetric bifurcations - all without active actuators. Anticipates claims to: passive geometric splitting of microfluidic droplets at channel branches with volume ratio set by branch hydrodynamic resistance; downstream-geometry control of droplet size from a single upstream generator; and passive bifurcation-based droplet sorting. Foundational droplet-handling-primitive paper from the A. P. Lee group, predating and complementing the Link 2004 geometric-breakup analysis.
notes: A. P. Lee group. Passive droplet splitting/sorting/dilution primitives; companion to link-2004-geometrically-mediated-drop-breakup.

canonical_name: Link 2004 geometrically mediated breakup of drops in microfluidic devices
disclosure_citation: Link, D. R.; Anna, S. L.; Weitz, D. A.; Stone, H. A. Geometrically mediated breakup of drops in microfluidic devices. Phys. Rev. Lett. 2004, 92, 054503. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.054503
creator: Weitz / Stone groups, Harvard
channel_geometry: symmetric and asymmetric T-shaped bifurcations and channel-spanning obstacles; drop break-up governed by extension and Rayleigh-Plateau-like instability; phase diagram in (initial drop extension, capillary number)
throughput: cascaded bifurcations generate 2^n droplets from one mother drop
notable_capabilities: phase diagram predicting whether a drop breaks or passes intact at a bifurcation
controlled binary splitting of drops at symmetric junctions; biased split at asymmetric ones
cascades of bifurcations produce large monodisperse populations from a single drop
obstacles in the channel used to trigger break-up
prior_art_notes: Provides the physics of geometrically mediated drop break-up: a drop entering a T-bifurcation either splits or passes intact depending on its initial extension and the capillary number, captured in a quantitative phase diagram, and cascaded bifurcations multiply one mother drop into 2^n monodisperse daughters; obstacles can likewise be used to trigger controlled break-up. Anticipates claims to: passive controlled splitting of microfluidic drops at channel bifurcations or obstacles with break/no-break governed by drop extension and capillary number; biased splitting at asymmetric junctions for volume metering; and cascaded-bifurcation droplet multiplication. Together with tan-2004-microfluidic-droplet-volume-channel-geometry it anchors passive droplet-splitting prior art. Weitz/Stone droplet lineage.
notes: Weitz/Stone (David Link later founded RainDance). Geometric drop-breakup phase diagram; companion to tan-2004.

canonical_name: Utada 2005 monodisperse double emulsions generated from a microcapillary device
aliases: Utada Lorenceau Link Kaplan Stone Weitz 2005
disclosure_citation: Utada, A. S.; Lorenceau, E.; Link, D. R.; Kaplan, P. D.; Stone, H. A.; Weitz, D. A. Monodisperse double emulsions generated from a microcapillary device. Science 2005, 308, 537-541. DOI: 10.1126/science.1109164
creator: David A. Weitz group, Harvard (with H. A. Stone)
channel_geometry: coaxial assembly of cylindrical glass capillaries inside a square capillary: tapered injection tube, collection tube; combined co-flow + flow-focusing geometry generating core-shell drops in one step
throughput: single-step generation of monodisperse W/O/W (or O/W/O) double emulsions; controlled number of inner drops per shell
notable_capabilities: one-step generation of monodisperse double emulsions with precise control of shell thickness and inner-drop count
glass-capillary device immune to PDMS wetting/swelling problems
template for microcapsules, controlled-release vehicles, and microfluidic synthesis of structured particles
dripping-to-jetting transition characterized
prior_art_notes: The seminal one-step monodisperse double-emulsion device: nested coaxial glass capillaries combining co-flow and flow-focusing so a core fluid is enveloped by a middle fluid and pinched into a continuous outer phase, producing core-shell drops with controllable shell thickness and a defined number of inner drops per shell. Anticipates claims to: glass-microcapillary co-flow/flow-focusing devices for single-step double (and higher-order) emulsion generation; monodisperse double emulsions as templates for microcapsules and controlled-release particles; and the dripping/jetting control of capillary droplet generators. Foundational for the entire structured-emulsion / microcapsule field and for double-emulsion single-cell assays (cf. brouzes-2009-droplet-screening). Weitz/Stone capillary-droplet lineage.
notes: Weitz lab glass-capillary droplet platform. HIGH-PRIORITY anchor: the canonical double-emulsion microfluidic device.

canonical_name: Song 2003 microfluidic system for controlling reaction networks in time (plug-based)
disclosure_citation: Song, H.; Tice, J. D.; Ismagilov, R. F. A microfluidic system for controlling reaction networks in time. Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2003, 42, 768-772. DOI: 10.1002/anie.200390203
creator: Rustem F. Ismagilov group, University of Chicago
channel_geometry: aqueous reagent streams co-injected with an immiscible carrier (fluorinated oil) at a junction to form nanoliter plugs; winding channels induce chaotic advection inside plugs for rapid mixing; plug spacing = time axis
sample_volume: nanoliter plugs
throughput: sub-millisecond mixing inside plugs; reaction time mapped to downstream channel position
notable_capabilities: plug-based (segmented-flow) microfluidics with no Taylor dispersion between plugs
rapid (<2 ms) internal mixing by chaotic advection in winding channels
reaction time encoded by distance traveled - turns a channel into a time axis
controlled merging of reagent plugs to initiate reactions on demand
prior_art_notes: Establishes plug-based (segmented-flow droplet) microfluidics for controlled reaction kinetics: aqueous reagents are compartmentalized into nanoliter plugs by an immiscible carrier fluid, internally mixed within milliseconds by chaotic advection in winding channels, and transported so that downstream position maps directly to reaction time - eliminating Taylor dispersion and enabling time-resolved chemistry/kinetics in a microchannel. Anticipates claims to: segmented-flow plug reactors for kinetic measurement with time encoded by channel length; rapid intra-plug mixing by serpentine-channel chaotic advection; and merging of distinct reagent plugs to trigger reactions. Foundational for the Ismagilov plug-microfluidics lineage (cf. du-ismagilov-2009-slipchip) and for droplet-based screening/crystallization generally.
notes: Ismagilov lab (Chicago, later Caltech). Origin of plug-based microfluidics; ancestor of SlipChip.

canonical_name: Du 2009 SlipChip
disclosure_citation: Du, W.; Li, L.; Nichols, K. P.; Ismagilov, R. F. SlipChip. Lab Chip 2009, 9, 2286-2292. DOI: 10.1039/b908978k
creator: Rustem F. Ismagilov group, University of Chicago
channel_geometry: two glass plates with patterned wells/ducts and intervening lubricant; relative sliding (slipping) of the plates re-routes connections, meters fluids, and initiates reactions in hundreds-to-thousands of nanoliter compartments simultaneously - no valves, no pumps
sample_volume: nanoliter to picoliter compartments
throughput: hundreds to thousands of parallel reactions/conditions set up by a single slip step
sensing: fluorescence / colorimetric / off-chip readout
notable_capabilities: valveless, pumpless metering and combinatorial routing by sliding two patterned plates
massively parallel multistep biochemistry (PCR, immunoassays, crystallization, digital quantification) without external instrumentation
digital PCR / digital LAMP by partitioning sample across an array of wells in one slip
field-deployable, instrument-light molecular diagnostics platform
prior_art_notes: Discloses the SlipChip: two plates bearing complementary patterns of wells and connecting ducts, separated by a lubricating fluid, where simple relative sliding re-routes which wells connect to which - thereby metering nanoliter aliquots, exposing reagents to one another, and initiating hundreds-to-thousands of reactions in parallel without any valves, pumps, or external control. Anticipates claims to: valveless/pumpless microfluidic metering and combinatorial fluid routing by relative translation of two patterned plates with an intervening immiscible lubricant; instrument-free multistep assay cartridges (PCR, immunoassay, crystallization screen) actuated by a slip motion; and digital nucleic-acid quantification by one-step partitioning of a sample into a well array. HIGH-PRIORITY anchor - the SlipChip underlies a family of instrument-light diagnostics and digital-assay products. Ismagilov plug/slip lineage (descends conceptually from song-ismagilov-2003-plug-based-reaction-networks).
notes: Ismagilov lab. HIGH-PRIORITY anchor: the SlipChip; valveless/pumpless plate-sliding microfluidics; basis of multiple diagnostics startups.

canonical_name: Yager 2006 microfluidic diagnostic technologies for global public health
aliases: Yager Edwards Fu Helton Nelson Tam Weigl 2006
disclosure_citation: Yager, P.; Edwards, T.; Fu, E.; Helton, K.; Nelson, K.; Tam, M. R.; Weigl, B. H. Microfluidic diagnostic technologies for global public health. Nature 2006, 442, 412-418. DOI: 10.1038/nature05064
creator: Paul Yager group, University of Washington (with PATH / Micronics)
sensing: colorimetric / fluorescence / lateral-flow readout
notable_capabilities: systematic framework (ASSURED-style) for point-of-care diagnostics in resource-limited settings
survey of laminate/paper/capillary microfluidic cartridges that need no instrumentation or power
H-filter and T-sensor diffusion-based separation/assay primitives for field use
blueprint that launched a generation of low-cost POC microfluidic devices
prior_art_notes: The seminal review of microfluidic diagnostics for the developing world: it lays out the design constraints for instrument-free, low-power, low-cost point-of-care testing (the ASSURED criteria), surveys laminate, paper, and capillary-driven cartridge architectures, and presents diffusion-based assay primitives (H-filter, T-sensor) suited to field use. As prior art it anticipates claims to: instrument-free capillary/laminate microfluidic diagnostic cartridges; integration of sample prep, reaction and colorimetric readout in a disposable card without external pumps; and the general system requirements of resource-limited-setting point-of-care microfluidics. HIGH-PRIORITY anchor - this paper essentially defined the low-cost-diagnostics microfluidics field and anchors paper-microfluidics, lateral-flow-plus-microfluidics, and instrument-light cartridge industries. Companion to brody-yager-1997-h-filter and whitesides-2010-mu-pads-systematic.
notes: Part of the 2006 Nature microfluidics insight issue. HIGH-PRIORITY anchor: the global-health POC-diagnostics manifesto.

canonical_name: El-Ali 2006 cells on chips
disclosure_citation: El-Ali, J.; Sorger, P. K.; Jensen, K. F. Cells on chips. Nature 2006, 442, 403-411. DOI: 10.1038/nature05063
creator: Klavs F. Jensen and Peter K. Sorger groups, MIT
sensing: on-chip optical microscopy / fluorescence
notable_capabilities: survey of microfluidics for cell biology: single-cell trapping, perfusion culture, stimulation, lysis, and high-content analysis
microfluidic gradient generators and dynamic-stimulus delivery for systems-biology measurements
integration of cell culture with downstream molecular assays on chip
argues microfluidics enables quantitative, time-resolved single-cell biology
prior_art_notes: The canonical Nature-insight review of cell biology on microfluidic chips: single-cell hydrodynamic and other trapping, perfusion culture with controlled microenvironments, microfluidic concentration-gradient generators, dynamic-stimulus delivery, on-chip lysis, and integration with downstream nucleic-acid/protein assays for systems-biology-grade single-cell measurements. As a unified prior-art statement it anticipates claims to: microfluidic perfusion culture with programmable soluble-factor gradients; integrated trap-stimulate-lyse-analyze workflows for single cells; and the broad concept of using microfluidics to make time-resolved, quantitative single-cell biology routine. Companion to di-carlo-2006-cell-trap-array and voldman-2002-cell-trap-dep-array. From the MIT Jensen/Sorger labs.
notes: Part of the 2006 Nature microfluidics insight issue (MIT Jensen/Sorger).

canonical_name: Craighead 2006 future lab-on-a-chip technologies for interrogating individual molecules
disclosure_citation: Craighead, H. Future lab-on-a-chip technologies for interrogating individual molecules. Nature 2006, 442, 387-393. DOI: 10.1038/nature05061
creator: Harold G. Craighead group, Cornell University
sensing: single-molecule fluorescence; zero-mode waveguides; nanopore current
notable_capabilities: survey of nanofluidic and single-molecule lab-on-chip: nanochannels, nanopores, zero-mode waveguides, entropic traps
DNA stretching/mapping in confining nanochannels
sub-diffraction optical confinement for single-molecule enzymology (ZMW)

disclosure_citation: BforCure SAS (Paris, France) Chronos Dx ultra-fast PCR platform disclosures and patents on a thin-film microfluidic cartridge enabling extremely rapid thermal cycling

flexible-film cartridge cheap to manufacture

canonical_name: binx health io Point-of-Care Molecular Cartridge (Chlamydia / Gonorrhea)

blister-pack on-cartridge reagent storage and valving
expanding menu (e.g. respiratory, other STIs)

Companion to cepheid-genexpert-cartridge and visby-medical entries (optical or strip readout) -- binx uses electrochemistry instead.

canonical_name: Quotient MosaiQ Microarray Blood-Typing and Disease-Screening Platform
disclosure_citation: Quotient Limited (Eysins, Switzerland / Edinburgh, UK) MosaiQ platform disclosures and patents on a microarray-based consumable for simultaneous blood grouping, antibody screening and infectious-disease serology

sensing: imaging readout of the reacted microarray (agglutination / labeled-binding spots); algorithmic interpretation of blood group and serology results
notable_capabilities: consolidated donor/patient testing: ABO/Rh/extended phenotype, antibody screen, and infectious-disease serology on one microarray consumable
microfluidic delivery and processing over a printed antigen/antibody array
reduced reagent volumes vs tube/gel-card immunohematology
transfusion-laboratory throughput

Companion to bio-rad-ih-1000-immunohematology (gel-card automation) -- MosaiQ uses a microarray instead of columns.
notes: Quotient Limited filed for bankruptcy / restructured in 2024; the MosaiQ consumable and IP remain citable prior art. Note the corporate status.

canonical_name: Thermo Fisher Accula (Mesa Biotech) Dock-and-Go Molecular POC Cartridge
disclosure_citation: Mesa Biotech (San Diego; acquired by Thermo Fisher Scientific 2021) Accula System disclosures and FDA-cleared/EUA molecular POC tests; patents on a lateral-flow-readout RT-PCR cartridge with a reusable dock

sample_volume: a swab eluate input; microliter-scale RT-PCR and lateral-flow volumes

notable_capabilities: true PCR sensitivity in a visually-read, instrument-light POC cassette
reusable thermal dock + disposable amplification/detection cassette
respiratory panel (SARS-CoV-2, Flu A/B, RSV) and strep menu
no reader optics required
prior_art_notes: Discloses a palm-sized RT-PCR cassette in which on-cassette amplification (heated by a reusable dock) is followed by lateral-flow amplicon detection with visual lines, achieving PCR sensitivity without reader optics. Anticipates: PCR-then-lateral-flow integrated POC cassettes; reusable-dock + disposable-amplification-cassette architectures. Companion to lucira-check-it-flu-covid-test and other strip-readout molecular POC entries.
notes: Mesa Biotech was acquired by Thermo Fisher Scientific in 2021; Accula continues under Thermo Fisher. The strip-readout PCR cassette is the inventive core.

canonical_name: Aptitude Medical Systems Metrix COVID-19 Molecular At-Home Test
disclosure_citation: Aptitude Medical Systems (Santa Barbara, California) Metrix COVID-19 Test disclosures and FDA-authorized over-the-counter molecular test; patents on a small isothermal-amplification cartridge with a reusable reader
creator: Aptitude Medical Systems
channel_geometry: a single-use test cup/cartridge with lyophilized isothermal-amplification reagents and a reaction chamber; a swab is swirled in the cartridge, the cap is closed, and a small reusable reader heats the chamber and reads a fluorescence/colorimetric signal; minimal user steps
sample_volume: a nasal-swab sample suspended in the cartridge buffer; microliter-scale reaction volume

sensing: fluorescence/colorimetric readout of the isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP-class chemistry) in the reusable reader; lay-user OTC workflow
notable_capabilities: low-cost over-the-counter molecular (not antigen) COVID-19 test
lyophilized reagents, simple swirl-and-close cartridge
reusable reader amortized over many disposable cartridges
expanding to other respiratory targets

Anticipates: consumer-grade isothermal molecular cartridges with reusable readers; minimal-user-step swab-in-cup molecular formats. Companion to lucira-check-it-flu-covid-test and detect-inc-covid-19-rt-lamp-cartridge.
notes: One of the few OTC-authorized molecular (vs antigen) home tests. Aptitude Medical Systems is a Santa Barbara aptamer/diagnostics company.

canonical_name: 3EO Health Low-Cost Molecular Point-of-Care Test (COVID-19 / Respiratory)
disclosure_citation: 3EO Health (Cambridge, Massachusetts) disclosures of a low-cost molecular POC test and FDA-cleared/authorized COVID-19 test; patents on an electrochemical-readout isothermal-amplification cartridge
creator: 3EO Health
channel_geometry: an inexpensive single-use cartridge with lyophilized isothermal-amplification reagents, a reaction chamber and screen-printed electrodes for electrochemical detection; a low-cost reusable reader provides heating and electrochemical interrogation; designed for very low per-test cost
sample_volume: a nasal-swab sample in cartridge buffer; microliter-scale reaction volume
throughput: molecular result in roughly 30 min, PCR-class sensitivity, at low cost

notable_capabilities: ultra-low-cost molecular POC via electrochemical (not optical) readout
lyophilized reagents and simple cartridge
cheap reusable reader

Companion to binx-health-io-molecular-poc-cartridge (also electrochemical) and to other low-cost-molecular-POC entries.
notes: Recent (2023-2024) entrant aiming at very low molecular-test cost via electrochemistry. draft pending verification of patent family.

canonical_name: Agilent 708-DS / 280-DS Dissolution Apparatus with Online UV Flow Cell
disclosure_citation: Agilent Technologies 708-DS Dissolution Apparatus and 280-DS automated sampling station datasheets; USP <711> Dissolution, Apparatus 1 (basket) and 2 (paddle) with online UV flow-cell detection
creator: Agilent Technologies

sample_volume: mL aliquots withdrawn per timepoint; UV flow cell internal volume on the order of tens of microliters
throughput: full dissolution profile of 6-8 vessels in parallel, automated timepoint sampling and readback

canonical_name: GeneFirst Multiplex PCR Cartridge (MeltArray Respiratory and Oncology Panels)
disclosure_citation: GeneFirst Ltd (Oxford / Wallingford, UK) MeltArray multiplex-PCR technology disclosures and PointLink cartridge / respiratory and EGFR oncology panel literature; patents on a melt-curve-multiplexed PCR assay

sample_volume: a swab/respiratory or plasma sample input; microliter-scale reaction volumes
throughput: broad respiratory (20+ pathogens) or oncology mutation panels in roughly 1-2 h from a few reaction wells

Companion to biofire-filmarray-multiplex-pcr-cartridge (spatial multiplexing) -- GeneFirst multiplexes in melt-temperature space instead.

canonical_name: Radioimmunoassay (RIA)
disclosure_citation: Yalow, R. S.; Berson, S. A. Immunoassay of endogenous plasma insulin in man. J. Clin. Invest. 1960, 39, 1157-1175. DOI: 10.1172/JCI104130
creator: Rosalyn Yalow, Solomon Berson (Veterans Administration Hospital, Bronx)
sample_volume: microliter-scale serum aliquots
notable_capabilities: competitive binding assay using radiolabeled antigen and limited antibody
picomolar sensitivity for plasma hormones
first quantitative immunoassay of a peptide hormone in human plasma
prior_art_notes: The foundational competitive-binding immunoassay. Discloses the core principle on which every downstream microfluidic immunoassay cartridge depends: a labeled tracer competing with analyte for a limited quantity of specific antibody, with bound/free separation read out as signal. Anticipates generic claims to competitive immunoassay architecture, labeled-tracer displacement readout, and standard-curve quantification of analyte concentration. The label has since migrated from radioisotope to enzyme (ELISA), fluorophore, and electrochemiluminescent tag, but the assay topology is unchanged. Any microfluidic device claiming novelty over competitive immunoassay as a category contends with this 1960 disclosure.
sources: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1977 (Yalow)
notes: Anchors the entire lineage of immunoassay-based point-of-care cartridges. Berson died in 1972; Yalow received the Nobel Prize in 1977.

canonical_name: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
disclosure_citation: Engvall, E.; Perlmann, P. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Quantitative assay of immunoglobulin G. Immunochemistry 1971, 8, 871-874. DOI: 10.1016/0019-2791(71)90454-X
creator: Eva Engvall, Peter Perlmann (Stockholm University); independently Van Weemen and Schuurs (Organon)
sample_volume: microliter-scale per well
notable_capabilities: enzyme-conjugated antibody replacing radioisotope label
solid-phase capture on polystyrene with chromogenic substrate readout
quantitative immunoglobulin measurement without radioactivity
prior_art_notes: Replaced the radioisotope of RIA with an enzyme conjugate (alkaline phosphatase, horseradish peroxidase) generating a colorimetric or fluorogenic product. Discloses the solid-phase sandwich and competitive ELISA topology that virtually every lateral-flow strip, microfluidic immunoassay chip, and bead-based multiplex assay implements at smaller scale. Anticipates: enzyme-amplified immunoassay readout, solid-phase antibody immobilization with washing steps, chromogenic/fluorogenic substrate conversion as the detection step. Microfluidic ELISA-on-chip devices (digital microfluidic ELISA, droplet ELISA, paper ELISA) are miniaturizations of this 1971 method and cannot claim the assay chemistry as novel.
sources: Van Weemen, B. K.; Schuurs, A. H. W. M. FEBS Lett. 1971, 15, 232-236
notes: Anchors all immunoassay cartridges and lateral-flow tests. Cuba SUMA, lateral-flow rapid tests, microfluidic ELISA chips all descend from this.

canonical_name: Hybridoma technology for monoclonal antibody production
disclosure_citation: Kohler, G.; Milstein, C. Continuous cultures of fused cells secreting antibody of predefined specificity. Nature 1975, 256, 495-497. DOI: 10.1038/256495a0
creator: Georges Kohler, Cesar Milstein (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge)
notable_capabilities: fusion of antibody-secreting B cell with immortal myeloma to yield a clonal antibody-producing cell line
production of unlimited quantities of a single antibody of defined specificity
deliberately not patented by the inventors
prior_art_notes: The source of essentially every monoclonal capture and detection antibody used in microfluidic immunoassays, lateral-flow strips, and bead-based multiplex panels. Kohler and Milstein famously did not patent the method (a decision later criticized in the UK). Anticipates generic claims to monoclonal-antibody-based affinity reagents and to clonal cell-line antibody manufacture. Any microfluidic diagnostic claiming novelty in its use of monoclonal antibody pairs as the recognition element contends with this disclosure as the enabling prior art for the reagent itself.
sources: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1984 (Kohler, Milstein, Jerne)
notes: Anchors all immunoassay reagent supply. Reagent-side ancestor of every immunoassay cartridge.

canonical_name: Sanger dideoxy chain-termination DNA sequencing
disclosure_citation: Sanger, F.; Nicklen, S.; Coulson, A. R. DNA sequencing with chain-terminating inhibitors. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 1977, 74, 5463-5467. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.74.12.5463
creator: Frederick Sanger, Steve Nicklen, Alan Coulson (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge)
notable_capabilities: polymerase extension terminated stochastically by dideoxynucleotides
size-separation of terminated fragments to read sequence
basis of capillary-array DNA sequencers and all sequencing sample-prep workflows
prior_art_notes: The dideoxy chain-termination method that all microfluidic and capillary-array DNA sequencing implements as the underlying chemistry. Anticipates: enzymatic primer extension with chain-terminating analogs, electrophoretic size-separation readout of the resulting ladder, and (in capillary form) the multiplexed-capillary sequencer architecture. Microfluidic sequencing-library-prep devices and lab-on-chip electrophoretic readers descend from this method; they cannot claim the sequencing chemistry as novel. Together with Mullis PCR 1985 it anchors the entire nucleic-acid-analysis branch of the corpus.
sources: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1980 (Sanger, his second)
notes: Public domain. Anchors all sequencing sample prep and capillary-array sequencers. Lineage ancestor of microfluidic library-prep chips.

canonical_name: Maxam-Gilbert chemical DNA sequencing
disclosure_citation: Maxam, A. M.; Gilbert, W. A new method for sequencing DNA. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 1977, 74, 560-564. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.74.2.560
creator: Allan Maxam, Walter Gilbert (Harvard University)
notable_capabilities: base-specific chemical cleavage of end-labeled DNA
gel-electrophoretic readout of cleavage fragments
the alternative foundational sequencing method to Sanger
prior_art_notes: The chemical-cleavage sequencing method that, alongside Sanger, established that DNA sequence could be read from a size-separated fragment ladder. Although largely superseded by enzymatic methods, it anticipates: base-specific chemical modification chemistry, end-labeling for fragment detection, and high-resolution electrophoretic ladder readout. Relevant prior art for any device claiming chemical-cleavage-based nucleic-acid analysis or footprinting on chip.
sources: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1980 (Gilbert, shared with Sanger and Berg)
notes: Public domain. The other 1977 sequencing method.

canonical_name: Southern blot (DNA transfer and hybridization)
disclosure_citation: Southern, E. M. Detection of specific sequences among DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis. J. Mol. Biol. 1975, 98, 503-517. DOI: 10.1016/S0022-2836(75)80083-0
creator: Edwin Southern (University of Edinburgh)
notable_capabilities: capillary transfer of size-separated DNA from gel to membrane
in situ hybridization with a labeled probe to detect specific sequences
template for Northern (RNA), Western (protein), and microarray hybridization formats
prior_art_notes: The original nucleic-acid transfer-and-hybridize protocol. Discloses capillary-driven transfer of biomolecules from a separation gel onto a binding membrane followed by probe hybridization for sequence-specific detection. Anticipates: membrane-immobilized target capture, labeled-probe hybridization detection, and (conceptually) the spotted DNA microarray. Microfluidic hybridization chambers, on-chip blotting devices, and integrated electrophoresis-plus-detection cartridges descend from this method. Eponymously named; the RNA, protein, and other variants are deliberately named after compass directions in homage.
notes: Public domain. Anchors all nucleic-acid transfer and hybridization-based detection, including microarrays.

canonical_name: Immunofluorescence (fluorescent antibody method)
disclosure_citation: Coons, A. H.; Creech, H. J.; Jones, R. N. Immunological properties of an antibody containing a fluorescent group. Proc. Soc. Exp. Biol. Med. 1941, 47, 200-202. DOI: 10.3181/00379727-47-13084P
creator: Albert Coons, Hugh Creech, Norman Jones (Harvard Medical School)
notable_capabilities: covalent conjugation of a fluorophore to an antibody preserving binding specificity
localization of antigen in tissue and cells by fluorescence microscopy
ancestor of all fluorescent immunoassay readouts
prior_art_notes: The first fluorescent-antibody conjugate. Discloses the principle that a fluorophore can be covalently attached to an immunoglobulin without destroying its specificity, enabling fluorescence as the readout of an antigen-antibody binding event. Anticipates: fluorophore-labeled detection antibodies, fluorescence-readout immunoassays, and (conceptually) flow-cytometric and microfluidic fluorescence immunodetection. Microfluidic immunoassay chips reading bound fluorescent conjugate descend from this method.
sources: Coons, A. H. et al. J. Immunol. 1942, 45, 159-170
notes: Public domain. Anchors fluorescent immunoassay and immunohistochemistry.

canonical_name: Moving-boundary electrophoresis (Tiselius apparatus)
disclosure_citation: Tiselius, A. A new apparatus for electrophoretic analysis of colloidal mixtures. Trans. Faraday Soc. 1937, 33, 524-531. DOI: 10.1039/tf9373300524
creator: Arne Tiselius (Uppsala University)
channel_geometry: U-shaped rectangular quartz cell, mm-scale bore
notable_capabilities: electrophoretic separation of serum proteins into albumin and alpha/beta/gamma globulin fractions
optical (Schlieren) detection of moving boundaries
first quantitative electrophoretic protein analysis
prior_art_notes: The founding apparatus of analytical electrophoresis. Tiselius separated serum proteins by mobility in free solution and detected the boundaries optically, establishing electrophoresis as a quantitative analytical separation. Anticipates: electrophoretic separation of biomolecules by charge-to-size ratio, optical detection of separated zones, and the entire conceptual basis of capillary and microchip electrophoresis. Every microfluidic CE chip, gel-on-chip, and isoelectric-focusing device traces to this method; the separation principle cannot be claimed as novel over it.
notes: Public domain. Anchors all electrophoretic separation, including microchip CE.

canonical_name: Analytical ultracentrifuge
disclosure_citation: Svedberg, T.; Rinde, H. The ultra-centrifuge, a new instrument for the determination of size and distribution of size of particle in amicroscopic colloids. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1924, 46, 2677-2693. DOI: 10.1021/ja01677a011
creator: The Svedberg, Herman Rinde (Uppsala University)
notable_capabilities: sedimentation of macromolecules under very high centrifugal fields
determination of molecular weight and size distribution from sedimentation velocity
defined the Svedberg unit of sedimentation coefficient
prior_art_notes: The instrument that established centrifugal sedimentation as a quantitative tool for sizing and separating macromolecules. Anticipates the conceptual and physical basis of all centrifugal sample-preparation: density-gradient separation, sediment-and-resuspend nucleic-acid prep, and centrifugal microfluidic (lab-on-a-disc) platforms where rotation supplies the body force for valving, mixing, and plasma separation. Any device claiming novelty in using centrifugal force for size-based separation of biological particles contends with this foundational disclosure.
notes: Public domain. Anchors centrifugal sample prep and lab-on-a-disc platforms.

canonical_name: Partition chromatography
disclosure_citation: Martin, A. J. P.; Synge, R. L. M. A new form of chromatogram employing two liquid phases. Biochem. J. 1941, 35, 1358-1368. DOI: 10.1042/bj0351358
creator: Archer Martin, Richard Synge (Wool Industries Research Association, Leeds)
notable_capabilities: separation by differential partition between a stationary liquid held on a solid support and a moving liquid phase
theoretical-plate treatment of column efficiency
ancestor of paper chromatography, GLC, and HPLC
prior_art_notes: Introduced partition (rather than adsorption) as the basis of chromatographic separation and the theoretical-plate model of column performance. Anticipates the operating principle of every microfluidic chromatography column, on-chip LC, and packed-bed separation device, plus the plate-height analysis used to characterize them. The 1941 paper also explicitly proposed gas as the mobile phase, anticipating gas chromatography. Microfluidic separation columns claiming novelty in partition-based retention contend with this disclosure.
notes: Public domain. Anchors all column chromatography including on-chip LC.

canonical_name: Paper partition chromatography
disclosure_citation: Consden, R.; Gordon, A. H.; Martin, A. J. P. Qualitative analysis of proteins: a partition chromatographic method using paper. Biochem. J. 1944, 38, 224-232. DOI: 10.1042/bj0380224
creator: Raphael Consden, Archer Gordon, Archer Martin (Wool Industries Research Association / Lister Institute)
channel_geometry: filter-paper sheet, capillary pore network
notable_capabilities: amino-acid and peptide separation on a filter-paper sheet by capillary-driven solvent flow
two-dimensional development for improved resolution
the original capillary-driven paper-based analytical separation
prior_art_notes: The direct ancestor of paper microfluidics. Discloses capillary-wicking transport of sample through a cellulose paper matrix as the engine of an analytical separation, including two-dimensional development. Anticipates: passive capillary-driven flow in paper as a microfluidic transport mechanism, paper as a substrate for multi-step analysis, and spot-detection readout. Every microPAD (microfluidic paper-based analytical device), lateral-flow strip, and wax-printed paper assay descends from this 1944 method; the use of paper capillarity as a fluid-handling primitive cannot be claimed as novel over it.
notes: Public domain. Anchors all paper microfluidics, microPADs, lateral-flow assays.

canonical_name: Adsorption column chromatography (Tsvet)
disclosure_citation: Tswett, M. Physikalisch-chemische Studien uber das Chlorophyll. Die Adsorptionen. Ber. Dtsch. Bot. Ges. 1906, 24, 316-323
creator: Mikhail Tsvet (Mikhail Tswett) (University of Warsaw)
channel_geometry: glass column packed with calcium carbonate adsorbent
notable_capabilities: separation of plant pigments into colored bands on a packed adsorbent column
coined the term chromatography (color writing)
first true chromatographic separation
prior_art_notes: The original chromatographic separation: differential adsorption of analytes onto a packed solid as a mobile solvent flows through, resolving a mixture into spatially distinct bands. Anticipates the operating principle of every packed-bed separation column, including microfluidic on-chip chromatography and solid-phase extraction beds used for sample cleanup in lab-on-chip cartridges. The conceptual foundation of all column separation; cannot be claimed as novel by any later chromatographic device.
sources: Tswett, M. Ber. Dtsch. Bot. Ges. 1906, 24, 384-393
notes: Public domain. The root of all chromatography. Tsvet was Italian-born, Russian-trained, worked in Warsaw (then Russian Empire).

canonical_name: Quantitative organic microanalysis
disclosure_citation: Pregl, F. Die quantitative organische Mikroanalyse. Springer, Berlin, 1917 (methods developed and presented from 1911; Nobel Prize 1923)
creator: Fritz Pregl (University of Graz / University of Innsbruck)
sample_volume: single-milligram samples; microliter-scale titrations
notable_capabilities: elemental analysis (C, H, N, S, halogens) on milligram rather than gram quantities
development of the microbalance and micro-combustion train
established that quantitative chemistry could be done at the sub-milligram scale
prior_art_notes: The methodological root of microscale quantitative analysis. By cutting sample requirements by roughly two orders of magnitude and developing the microbalance and micro-combustion apparatus, Pregl established the premise that underlies all of microfluidics: that complete quantitative analysis can be performed on vanishingly small samples. While not microfluidic in the channel sense, it is the conceptual ancestor cited when arguing that miniaturized total analysis is an incremental scaling of a century-old program rather than a novel paradigm. Relevant background prior art for claims framing micro-volume quantitative analysis as inherently novel.
sources: Pregl, F. Die quantitative organische Mikroanalyse. Springer, 1917
notes: Public domain. The microliter-scale analysis tradition microfluidics descends from. Builds on Emich.

canonical_name: Quantitative microchemical analysis (Emich method)
disclosure_citation: Emich, F. Lehrbuch der Mikrochemie. Wiesbaden, 1911 (methods from circa 1900); see Emich, F. Methoden der Mikrochemie. Z. Anal. Chem. 1910, 49, 1-25
creator: Friedrich Emich (Graz University of Technology)
sample_volume: microliter to sub-microliter droplets
notable_capabilities: chemical reactions and identifications performed on microscope-slide-scale droplets
micro-apparatus (capillary tubes, micro-test-tubes) for handling tiny volumes
the precursor discipline to quantitative organic microanalysis
prior_art_notes: An early systematization of chemistry done at the microliter and sub-microliter scale, including purpose-built micro-apparatus (capillaries, micro-vessels, microscope-slide reaction spots). Conceptual ancestor of spot-test microfluidics and droplet-scale chemistry. Cited as background prior art establishing that handling and reacting microliter volumes in dedicated small-scale glassware is a discipline more than a century old; relevant to claims framing droplet-scale or slide-scale chemical analysis as fundamentally new.
notes: Public domain. Emich and his student Pregl founded the Graz school of microchemistry.

canonical_name: Microchemical analysis (Behrens crystal-test method)
disclosure_citation: Behrens, H. Anleitung zur mikrochemischen Analyse. Voss, Hamburg/Leipzig, 1894-1897
